title: Policies
heading: Policies
start_phrase: The Group’s Code of Ethics is the document that governs the guiding principles, values and rules of conduct that complement the legal and regulatory obligations for workers in the upstream value chain.
summary:
- Scope and focus: Addresses workers in the upstream value chain only, covering working conditions and other labour-related rights identified as material impacts.
- Core policies:
  - Group Code of Ethics governs supplier conduct, requiring explicit acceptance and alignment; emphasizes fairness, transparency, integrity, and avoidance of conflicts of interest; commits to UN Universal Declaration of Human Rights, including principles on Child and Forced Labour.
  - Organisation, Management and Control Model pursuant to Italian Legislative Decree 231/2001 guides supplier selection and prohibits relationships without 231 compliance.
  - Procurement approach prioritizes occupational health and safety and environmental protection; supported by Group Health & Safety Policy (aligned with UNI ISO 45001) and Group Sustainability & ESG Policy integrating ESG into strategy, risk indicators, and stakeholder engagement.
  - Governance: Policies approved/overseen by the Board and top management; references to recognized standards (ISO 45001, IDD, MiFID 2 ESG); documents available on the corporate website/intranet.
  - Stakeholder engagement with suppliers managed by the Purchasing Department.
- Actions and controls:
  - Supplier pre-qualification and contracting include checks on labour law compliance, application of National Collective Labour Agreements, DURC (contribution regularity), ESG certifications, 231 compliance statements, anti-mafia documentation, and alignment of supplier Codes of Ethics.
  - Heightened due diligence for categories where worker protection is critical (authorizations, safety measures, training).
  - 100% of counterparties informed of anti-corruption policies and procedures.
  - Annual updates and document reviews for suppliers’ social sustainability; Purchasing Department manages Supplier Register qualification.
  - Control functions assess data protection programs of suppliers; privacy roles and clauses embedded in contracts.
  - No serious human rights incidents reported in the upstream value chain.
- Monitoring, metrics, and targets:
  - No specific quantitative targets yet for value chain workers; effectiveness ensured via indicators, Supplier Register re-verifications, and Control/Internal Audit activities.
  - In 2024, 100% of new suppliers (114) were assessed against environmental criteria in line with international standards; continuous verification for each new supplier.
  - Future evaluation of setting specific targets to drive continuous improvement.
- Compliance status: No detected cases of non-compliance with the UN Guiding Principles, ILO Declaration, or OECD Guidelines regarding upstream workers.
text:
Policies
The Group’s Code of Ethics is the document that governs the guiding principles, values and rules of conduct that complement  
the legal and regulatory obligations for workers in the upstream value chain. The Group is committed to fostering the  
adoption of the same among its subsidiaries, associates, business partners, consultants and collaborators in order  
to guide behaviour based on ethical and professional standards. 
This document reflects the Group’s commitment to structuring relations with its suppliers based on fairness and  
transparency. Transparency, cooperation, fairness and integrity are also promoted, avoiding situations of conflict of  
interest or unlawful behaviour.
Application of the Code is ensured through the internal control system, which is an essential element of the overall gover-
nance system of a company. More specifically, suppliers are sensitised to providing their services in line with standards 
of conduct consistent with those indicated in the Code of Ethics. In fact, on the basis of contracts and general purchasing 
conditions, suppliers are required to expressly accept, by means of a specific form, the declaration of commitment not to 
engage in behaviour that conflicts with the provisions of the Group’s Code of Ethics. Therefore, suppliers, in compliance  
with their contractual purchasing conditions, are directed to respect the rights of their workers and the responsible  
handling of any resulting social criteria. The Group also undertakes to respect the United Nations Universal Declaration 
of Human Rights, promoting the protection of human rights, including the principles on Child Labour and Forced Labour. 
For more details on the Group’s Code of Ethics, please refer to the section “Policies, Actions and Targets on Business  
Conduct” in “Section 4 - Governance Information”.
The Group also respects, in its relations with upstream value chain actors, the dictates of the Organisation, Management 
and Control Model for the prevention of offences pursuant to Legislative Decree 231/01, which lays down strict rules  
of conduct to be observed in the selection of the supply chain. The Group is also committed to selecting its suppliers  
by considering occupational health and safety related aspects and promoting joint initiatives for management and the  
resolution of any risk situations with a view to mutual cooperation. It is also committed to adopting a procurement policy  
that protects the health and safety of workers, the environment and people in general. Working conditions are also  
safeguarded by Group MPS’s Occupational Health and Safety Policy and the Group’s Sustainability and ESG Policy.
The constant involvement of suppliers, in order to ensure the protection of their interests, takes place through the Stakeholder  
Management process overseen by the Purchasing Department. For more details on stakeholder engagement, please refer 
to “Section 1 - General Information” of this document on the “Stakeholder Engagement” process.
To date, no cases of non-compliance with the UN Guiding Principles, the ILO Declaration or the OECD Guidelines with  
regard to workers in the upstream value chain have been detected at Group level.BANCA MONTE DEI PASCHI DI SIENA210Policies Description

title: Actions
heading: Actions
start_phrase: The following initiatives involve the majority of the Group’s suppliers and external service providers, including professionals, companies and foreign businesses, and are part of the Group’s normal practice regarding the management of supply relationships.
summary:
- Scope and context: Initiatives cover most suppliers and external providers (including foreign businesses) as part of routine supply relationship management; double materiality analysis found only potential, not actual, negative impacts.
- Supplier selection and compliance: Suppliers are evaluated during pre-selection, award, and contract finalization for compliance with labor regulations, National Collective Labour Agreement application, DURC (Single Document of Contribution Regularity), ESG certifications, and alignment with the Group’s Code of Ethics (counterparties’ Codes must not conflict).
- Mandatory documentation: During registration, suppliers provide the 231 Model Compliance Statement (including anti-corruption references) and anti-mafia documentation, plus responses on certifications and ethics; new lawyers must sign contractual documentation.
- Model 231 requirements: Suppliers must declare knowledge of and compliance with Legislative Decree 231/2001; for higher-risk product categories, enhanced due diligence covers economic/financial soundness, permits/authorizations, worker safety measures, and specialized training.
- Anti-corruption and data protection: 100% of suppliers with commercial relations are informed of anti-corruption policies; Control functions annually verify suppliers’ data protection programs, and contracts include privacy role clauses.
- Governance and monitoring: Purchasing Department leads collection/verification for Supplier Register enrollment; annual checks ensure updated social sustainability documentation; Control and Internal Audit functions perform oversight.
- Human rights: No serious human rights issues reported in the upstream value chain to date.
- Objectives and performance: No specific targets yet for value chain workers; effectiveness ensured via indicators, post-contractual re-verification of Supplier Register requisites, and control/audit activities. In 2024, 100% of new suppliers (114) were assessed against environmental criteria aligned with international standards; continuous verification applies to each new supplier. Future adoption of specific targets is under evaluation.
text:
Actions
The following initiatives involve the majority of the Group’s suppliers and external service providers, including  
professionals, companies and foreign businesses, and are part of the Group’s normal practice regarding the management 
of supply relationships. It should also be noted that the material impacts identified in the double materiality analysis  
are potential, therefore, to date, the Group has not had to intervene to remedy any actual negative impacts.
The Group is committed to adopting standards of supplier selection and management in order to encourage compliance 
with social and human rights criteria throughout the supply chain. Suppliers are selected based on an assessment process 
that, in the pre-selection, award and supply contract finalisation stage and through specific questions, explicitly assesses 
compliance with regulations on labour law, National Collective Labour Agreement application, payment of contributions 
(DURC) as certified by the Single Document of Contribution Regularity (hereinafter also DURC) the possession of ESG  
certification of the counterparty. Furthermore during the registration phase, the acquisition of documents concerning the 
231 model Compliance Statement (with references to anti-corruption legislation) and anti-mafia legislation is required, 
with specific questions on certification and the Code of Ethics. The provisions of the Code of Ethics that the counterparty 
may have must not conflict with the provisions of the Group Code of Ethics.
The 231 Model of the Group, which generally oversees relations with partners, does not allow relations with suppliers 
unless they declare and guarantee that they know and will comply with Legislative Decree 231/2001. For specific product  
categories, where protecting workers’ physical wellbeing and moral character is of key importance, the commitment  
focuses strongly on examining the supplier’s economic and financial conditions and the level of protection for workers. 
To achieve this, investigative tools are used to check that authorisations and permits have been issued, prevention and 
safety measures have been adopted and specialised training has been provided. The individual suppliers are informed 
of the Group anti-corruption policies and procedures, covering 100% of suppliers with which it has commercial relations.
At the same time, at Group level, checks are conducted on an annual basis to verify any updates in the documentation 
that the supplier counterparty has made available to the Group regarding its social sustainability. This process makes it 
possible to monitor whether suppliers have not met their obligations at the time of registration in the Group’s Suppliers 
Register. In addition, if a new lawyer is appointed, she/he must sign contractual documentation. The Group has identified  
the Purchasing Department as the function dedicated, on a priority basis, to collecting the documentation and verifying the 
existence of supplier requisites, for the purpose of registration in the Group’s Supplier Register.
Verification activities are carried out by the Control functions concerning the extent and compliance of the data protection 
programmes used by the Group’s suppliers and business partners. Moreover, data protection is also ensured in contractual 
arrangements or cooperation agreements with third parties by envisaging specific clauses that identify the privacy roles 
accepted by each party.
Based on the analyses carried out by the functions involved, no serious human rights problems or incidents in the upstream  
value chain have been reported to date.

title: Objectives
heading: Objectives
start_phrase: The Group has not, to date, defined any specific targets to deal with the issue of value chain workers.
summary:
- Focus: Management of supplier and external service provider relationships across the Group within the sustainability framework; double materiality analysis indicates only potential impacts to date, with no actual negative impacts requiring remediation.

- Supplier selection and compliance: Multi-stage assessment (pre-selection, award, contract finalization) includes checks on labor law compliance, National Collective Labour Agreement application, DURC (contribution regularity), ESG certifications, Model 231 (Legislative Decree 231/2001) and anti-mafia compliance, and alignment with the Group Code of Ethics. All suppliers are informed of anti-corruption policies and procedures (100% coverage).

- Heightened due diligence for certain categories: For products/services where worker health, safety, and dignity are critical, the Group assesses suppliers’ financial soundness, authorizations/permits, prevention and safety measures, and specialized training.

- Governance and controls: The Purchasing Department manages documentation collection and verification for the Suppliers Register; annual updates of suppliers’ social sustainability documentation; Control and Internal Audit functions conduct monitoring. Data protection compliance of suppliers/partners is verified and reinforced via contractual privacy roles and clauses.

- Monitoring and outcomes: No serious human rights problems reported in the upstream value chain. While no specific targets for value chain workers are set yet, effectiveness is tracked through indicators, ongoing verifications after initial contracting, and internal controls. In 2024, 100% of new suppliers (114) were assessed against environmental criteria aligned with international standards; setting explicit targets will be evaluated in the future.

- Worker involvement: No formal engagement process with suppliers’ workers; indirect assessment via supplier questionnaires, scoring that favors certified suppliers, and self-certification of adoption of applicable national/regional collective agreements.

- Grievance and remediation: An open Whistleblowing system is available to external parties and supplier personnel to report violations of laws, internal rules, procedures, and the Code of Ethics, with safeguards for whistleblowers referenced elsewhere in the report.
text:
Objectives
The Group has not, to date, defined any specific targets to deal with the issue of value chain workers. 
However, the effectiveness of the policies and actions adopted in this regard is ensured through the monitoring of specific 
indicators in order to ensure supply chain management aimed at respecting the principles of social and environmental 
sustainability. In this regard, a the verification, in the years following those of the first contractualisation, of the existence of 
the requisites for registration in the Group’s Supplier Register, as well as the controls carried out by the Control and Internal  
Audit functions, guarantee the effectiveness of the policies and actions undertaken by the Group to protect the rights  
of workers in the upstream value chain and to pursue the development of relations with suppliers marked by respect  
for the human rights of their workers. 
During 2024, 100% of the new suppliers (114 in total) were assessed according to environmental criteria, in accordance 
with international standards. The verification activity described is carried out continuously in relation to each new supplier.
The adoption of specific targets to deal with this issue will be evaluated in the future to ensure continuous improvement  
of the Group’s commitment to workers in the value chain.BANCA MONTE DEI PASCHI DI SIENA212

title: Process of involving workers in the value chain on impacts
heading: Process of involving workers in the value chain on impacts
start_phrase: Although the Group does not have a formalised process for involving suppliers’ workers, either directly or through representatives, it does believe that the requirements assessed when signing contracts with suppliers make it indirectly possible to assess respect for the rights of the suppliers’ workers.
summary:
- The Group lacks a formal process to directly involve suppliers’ workers or their representatives but indirectly assesses respect for their rights through supplier onboarding and evaluation.
- During supplier evaluation, a questionnaire assesses qualifications, with certified suppliers receiving higher scores that influence contract awards.
- At registration, suppliers must self-certify adoption of applicable national/regional collective labor agreements.
- To address and remediate potential negative impacts on workers in the value chain, the Group offers accessible reporting channels, notably a Whistleblowing system open to external parties.
- The Whistleblowing system supports compliance with laws, internal regulations, and the Code of Ethics, reinforcing sustainability, integrity, and fairness.
- Access is available via institutional channels to non-Group employees, including staff of companies providing goods or services to the Group; details on protections and effectiveness are provided in the “Protection of Whistleblowers” section within Governance Information.
text:
Process of involving workers in the value chain on impacts
Although the Group does not have a formalised process for involving suppliers’ workers, either directly or through  
representatives, it does believe that the requirements assessed when signing contracts with suppliers make it indirectly 
possible to assess respect for the rights of the suppliers’ workers.
In particular, in the supplier evaluation stage, a questionnaire is submitted, with answers where the supplier with certification  
is given a score. Suppliers with certification obtain scores that also carry more weight in the selection process for the 
award of the supply/service.
In the registration stage, all suppliers are also asked to self-certify the adoption (where applicable) of national/regional 
collective agreements.

title: Processes to remediate negative impacts and channels for workers in the value chain to raise concerns
heading: Processes to remediate negative impacts and channels for workers in the value chain to raise concerns
start_phrase: In order to prevent and/or remedy the concerns of workers in the value chain, the Group provides channels of free access also to external parties, such as the Whistleblowing system.
summary:
- Supplier and value-chain worker involvement: The Group lacks a formalized process to directly engage suppliers’ workers, but indirectly assesses respect for their rights through supplier onboarding and selection. A questionnaire-based supplier evaluation gives higher scores and weight to certified suppliers, and all suppliers must self-certify adoption of applicable national/regional collective agreements.

- Remediation and grievance channels: A free-access Whistleblowing system is available to internal and external parties, including employees of suppliers and third-party contractors. It supports risk prevention, compliance with laws and internal rules, and upholds the Code of Ethics, contributing to sustainability and integrity. Protections for whistleblowers are detailed in the Governance section.

- Affected communities (ESRS S3): Using a double materiality approach, the Group mapped impacts, risks, and opportunities by reviewing internal/public documentation and existing initiatives (e.g., cultural, scientific, social, environmental programs; youth employability and work-orientation activities; collaborations with local institutions; support for the agri-food sector). Material outcomes identified include:
  - Positive impacts in own operations from initiatives that protect and enhance territories (urban, cultural) and promote youth employability.
  - Positive downstream impacts from actions supporting employability in key national sectors.
  - Opportunities in the downstream value chain to expand products and services that support companies in sectors critical to the national economy, including financing for the national production fabric.
  - Relevant scopes span own operations and the downstream value chain. Policies, actions, and targets on territorial impacts are indicated to follow in subsequent sections.
text:
Processes to remediate negative impacts and channels for workers in the value chain to raise concerns
In order to prevent and/or remedy the concerns of workers in the value chain, the Group provides channels of free access 
also to external parties, such as the Whistleblowing system. This system helps control and prevent the risks that the Group 
may face due to facts and actions that are contrary to external rules, company regulations, internal procedures and its 
Code of Ethics contributing to the implementation of sustainability policies, promoting integrity and fairness.
Moreover, access is through institutional channels, and therefore the system may also be accessed by any employees  
or staff not only of the Group, such as employees belonging to companies that provide goods or services or perform  
work for third parties and perform or have performed their work for the Group. For more details on the effectiveness  
of the Whistleblowing system, as well as on the safeguards and protection measures for whistleblowers, please refer to  
the section “Protection of Whistleblowers” within Section 4 - Governance Information of this document.2024 ANNUAL REPORT - Sustainability Reporting 213

start_phrase: The process to map impacts, risks and opportunities with reference to this standard includes the specific aspects related to the Group’s operations.
summary:
- Focus: ESRS S3 Affected communities within the 2024 Sustainability Report of Banca Monte dei Paschi di Siena, covering impacts, risks, opportunities, policies, actions, and monitoring processes tied to community-related topics.
- Materiality results: Double materiality analysis identified:
  - Positive impacts in own operations through support to local communities via urban enhancement, cultural initiatives, and youth employability.
  - Positive impacts in the downstream value chain via actions supporting employability in key national sectors.
  - Opportunities in the downstream value chain to broaden products and services that support companies in strategic sectors of the national economy; community engagement may also create financing opportunities for the national production fabric.
- Mapping process: Based on internal and public documentation, identifying initiatives protecting and enhancing communities (e.g., cultural, scientific, social, environmental activities; work orientation; partnerships with local institutions for sustainable growth).
- Scope: Emphasis on own operations for territorial/community support and downstream value chain for employability and product/service expansion; upstream value chain not highlighted as material in the excerpt.
- Territory-related impacts: The Group aims to support urban, cultural, and youth employment dimensions and certain economic sectors through dedicated policies, processes, and safeguards.
- Governance and oversight: Policies ensure structured planning, authorization, and oversight of community-related activities, with roles for Top Management and the Board of Directors.
- Key policies described:
  - Group Directive on Communication and External Affairs: Sets governance for external communication (media, social media, events, sponsorships, heritage), requires approvals, aligns with Italian legal/regulatory provisions (Legislative Decree 39/2010, ABI Circular 15/2010, Bank of Italy Circular 285/2013), and is accessible to all employees.
  - Historical Archive Management: Regulates creation, archiving, and transfer of documents of historical interest; supervised by the Archival Superintendency for Tuscany; aligned with the Code of Cultural Heritage (Legislative Decree 42/2004) and includes safeguards to prevent liability under Legislative Decree 231/2001 for cultural heritage offences; accessible to employees.
  - Artistic Heritage Management: Governs cataloguing, preservation, enhancement, and protection of the Bank’s artistic movable assets per Legislative Decree 42/2004 and the Italian Constitution; managed by the Historical and Artistic Heritage function; accessible to employees.
- Monitoring: The section indicates the Group monitors the effectiveness of policies and actions related to material impacts and opportunities, with further details to follow in subsequent paragraphs.
text:
The process to map impacts, risks and opportunities with reference to this standard includes the specific aspects related  
to the Group’s operations. In fact, several initiatives aimed at protecting the communities of reference are underway 
and planned, which could generate positive impacts on them. These impacts relate, for example, to cultural, scientific,  
social and environmental initiatives, work orientation activities and collaborations with local institutions for the  
sustainable growth of productive fabrics. Interaction with communities could also entail opportunities for the Group  
related to the provision of financing to support companies belonging to the national production fabric.
The mapping process included the analysis of the Group’s internal and public documentation and the identification of  
initiatives taken to protect communities (e.g. support to the agri-food sector) that could be materially impacted by the 
Group. On the basis of the analyses performed, the following were material: 
• Positive impacts with reference to the Own Operations  perimeter related to the support to communities through initiatives  
aimed at protecting and enhancing the territory in which they reside from an urban, cultural and youth employability 
point of view, and with reference to the Downstream Value Chain perimeter for the actions undertaken to support  
employability in some key sectors at a national level;
• Opportunities  related to the Downstream Value Chain perimeter related to the expansion of the range of products  
and services aimed at supporting companies operating in key sectors for the national economy.

summary:

  - Define roles, approval flows and oversight by Top Management/Board.
  - Align with Italian regulations and sector standards (e.g., Legislative Decree 39/2010, ABI Circular 15/2010, Bank of Italy Circular 285/2013, Legislative Decree 42/2004, Legislative Decree 231/2001 as amended by Law 22/2022).
  - Are accessible to employees via the corporate intranet.
- Community development aims: Professional development and orientation, financial education, support for vulnerable groups, and enhancement of banking and national artistic heritage.
- MPS Orienta program (2024): Career guidance, soft-skills development, financial education, and school–university engagement to strengthen the education–work bridge and employer branding.
  - Agreements with universities, master’s and specialist schools nationwide for curricular and non-curricular internships.
  - 40 internships activated in specialized functions (avg. 6 months), with some hires.
  - Participation in 2 University of Siena career days.
  - Education benefits for employees/families via Unitelma: 43 undergraduate and 184 post-graduate enrollments since 2020; agreement renewed for 2025–26.
- Support to the agri-food sector: Tailored financial services and strategic advisory to bolster local business sustainability.
  - MPS AgriDOP supports ecological transition and PDO/PGI, organic and environmental certifications; long-term value-chain and consortium support.

heading: MPS Orienta
start_phrase: In 2024, in line with previous years, the Group also implemented the MPS Orienta programme, focusing on career guidance, the development of soft skills, financial education and, in general, relations with schools and universities.
summary:
- Focus: Group actions to manage land-related impacts through student career guidance, support for the agri-food sector in its operating areas, and promotion of cultural initiatives in the arts.

- MPS Orienta 2024:
  - Objectives: career guidance, soft-skill development, financial education, employer branding, stronger school–work links, support for national socio-economic development and sustainable growth, and closer customer–territory relations.
  - Key initiatives:
    - Conventions with universities, master’s and specialization schools enabling curricular and extracurricular internships aligned with studies.
    - 40 traineeships in 2024 in specialized functions (avg. 6 months), some leading to employment.
    - Participation in two University of Siena career days with job orientation and internship presentations.
    - Agreement with Unitelma (La Sapienza’s online university) for subsidized online degrees for employees and family members; since 2020 (renewed for 2025–26): 43 undergraduate and 184 Level I/II postgraduate enrollments.

- Support for the agri-food sector:
  - Tailored financial products and ongoing strategic advisory through specialized centers in major Italian agrifood districts to bolster community and business sustainability.
  - MPS AgriDOP: long-term program aiding ecological transition of companies, especially in the “DOP Economy” (PDO/PGI) and those with organic/environmental certifications, aligned with the EU Green Deal and circular-economy goals.
  - Expansion of Agrifood Centres from 15 to 21 nationwide, offering specialized advisors and a distinctive mix from financing to protection solutions.
  - Proactive advisory to identify subsidies, develop impactful projects, and guide firms toward innovation, digitalization, and sustainability in line with the NRRP.

- Sector engagement and partnerships:
  - Sponsorship and participation in key industry events: Gambero Rosso’s Guida Oli d’Italia 2024, Vinitaly, the MASAF-organized States General of National and International Olive Growing, and Divinazione Expo (which hosted the G7 Agriculture).
text:
MPS Orienta
In 2024, in line with previous years, the Group also implemented the MPS Orienta programme, focusing on career guidance, 
the development of soft skills, financial education and, in general, relations with schools and universities.
The initiatives aim to promote employer branding, strengthen the link between education and the world of work, support 
the country’s economic and social development, contribute to sustainable growth strategies and strengthen relations  
with customers and the area in which the Group operates.
The main initiatives of the MPS Orienta programme in 2024 include:
• Conventions and framework agreements with universities, masters and specialisation schools throughout the country: 
these arrangements allow young graduates or undergraduates to carry out curricular and non-curricular internships in 
specialist functions consistent with their studies;
• Traineeships with the Group: 40 traineeships in specialised facilities were activated in 2024, with an average duration of 
6 months, some of which ended with employment;
• Career days: the Group participated in the 2 career days organised by the University of Siena with job orientation inter -
views and presentation of open internship positions;
• Arrangements for employees and their family members: An arrangement targeting Group employees and their family mem-
bers has been signed with Unitelma (the online university of La Sapienza, Rome) for subsidised enrolment in online graduate  
and post-graduate courses. Since the signing of the agreement in 2020 and its renewal for the two-year period 2025-26,  
43 enrolments in undergraduate courses and 184 enrolments in Level I and II post-graduate courses have been recorded.

title: The Group and support for the agri-food business
heading: The Group and support for the agri-food business
start_phrase: In order to support the agri-food component of the reality in which it operates, also in 2024 the Group set the objective of specialising its products and services to support the sustainability of the community and businesses, with made-to-measure financial services and constant strategic support, through a network of specialised centres in Italy’s main agrifood districts.
summary:
- Focus and scope: The section outlines Banca Monte dei Paschi di Siena’s 2024 actions to manage land-related impacts through education and employability initiatives, targeted support to the agri-food sector, tourism development, and promotion of green energy, with an overarching aim of sustainable growth and stronger ties to local communities.

- MPS Orienta (education and employability):
  - Continued programmes on career guidance, soft skills, and financial education; employer branding and school–university relations.
  - University agreements enabling curricular and extra-curricular internships in specialist functions.
  - 40 internships activated (avg. 6 months), some leading to employment.
  - Participation in two University of Siena career days.
  - Employee/family education benefits with Unitelma: since 2020 (renewed for 2025–26), 43 undergraduate and 184 postgraduate enrollments.

- Agri-food sector support:
  - Expansion and specialisation of products/services to foster community and business sustainability.
  - MPS AgriDOP: long-term support to PDO/PGI and certified supply chains, aiding ecological transition and alignment with EU Green Deal and circular economy.
  - Agrifood Centres expanded from 15 to 21 across key districts, offering specialised advisory, financing, protection solutions, and guidance on subsidies; focus on innovation, digitalisation, and sustainability in line with NRRP.
  - Events and partnerships: sponsorship of Gambero Rosso’s Guida Oli d’Italia 2024; participation in Vinitaly; “Stati Generali dell’olivicoltura” (MASAF); Divinazione Expo alongside G7 Agricoltura.
  - New dedicated product: “Finanziamento Impiantolivo” with direct Ismea guarantee for olive grove and mill investments.
  - Memoranda/agreements: Assocamerestero (operational committee and sessions), Ministry of Agriculture (food sovereignty/forestry), Region of Sicily (Agriculture Dept.), Simec (credit mediation), Coldiretti/CIB (biogas).
  - Participation in MASAF–CDP agreements for Supply Chain Agreements (IV and V calls): in 2024, 198 loan extensions/new resolutions totaling ~EUR 124m; 47 stipulations for ~EUR 31m. Beneficiary distribution: South 68% (41% of resources), Centre 18% (20%), North 15% (39%).
  - Strengthened ties with protection consortia: 23 bank relationships with PDO/PGI consortia, enabling ~1,900 relationships with member companies.

- Tourism development:
  - Adherence to ABI–CDP–Ministry of Tourism agreement for the Fondo Rotativo Imprese to promote energy upgrades, environmental sustainability, and digital innovation in hospitality.
  - 11 initiatives financed in 2024 and 4 more in early 2025, for total investments exceeding EUR 41m.

- Green energy transition:
  - Launch of MPS Energia Verde business line to support companies and households in renewable energy adoption and energy efficiency.
  - Offer of dedicated, flexible financial solutions, specialist consultancy, partner networks, and support to access NRRP incentives.
text:
The Group and support for the agri-food business
In order to support the agri-food component of the reality in which it operates, also in 2024 the Group set the objective of 
specialising its products and services to support the sustainability of the community and businesses, with made-to-measure 
financial services and constant strategic support, through a network of specialised centres in Italy’s main agrifood districts. 
In this context, the Group continued to promote MPS AgriDOP , a project designed to support companies in the ecological 
transition, through the development of dedicated services and products, with a special focus on companies operating in 
the “DOP Economy” sector46. The initiative is based on a long-term strategy to support production chains and protection 
consortia oriented towards the valorisation of PDO or PGI products and organic or environmental certification (e.g. ecolo -
gical transition, launch of the European Green Deal programme aimed at achieving technological innovation and a circular, 
efficient and sustainable economy).
The network, designed to support and work alongside agricultural business owners (and likewise craftsmen, traders and 
tourism operators in the agrifood supply chain) in choosing financing, has expanded from 15 to 21 Agrifood Centres lo-
cated throughout Italy in the strongest agricultural areas, with specialised advisors and a distinctive product mix (from 
financing to protection policies).
In addition to taking a series of specific actions to support target companies by activating and developing ad hoc initiatives 
and campaigns, the Centres play a proactive and advisory role in identifying and analysing the subsidy measures available 
in the area of competence, favouring the development of projects that have a positive impact on business development. 
Support from sector experts and solutions are also offered to guide companies towards a development process characte -
rised by innovation, digitalisation and sustainability, which are central elements of the NRRP , are also offered.
The year 2024 also saw the Parent Company’s participation in events and the collaborations with important partners, in-
cluding sponsorship of the Guida Oli d’Italia 2024 promoted by Gambero Rosso, participation in the Vinitaly event in April 
and the “Stati Generali dell’olivicoltura nazionale ed internazionale” (States General of National and International Olive 
Growing) event, the latter organised by the Ministry of Agricultural, Food and Forestry Policies MASAF, and participation in 
Divinazione Expo (21-29 September), within which the G7 Agricoltur a (Agriculture G7) took place. 
46 Segment of the production and processing of agricultural products for food with geographical indications, which constitutes an important part of the 
national agri-food value.2024 ANNUAL REPORT - Sustainability Reporting 217In addition to collaboration and participation in dedicated events, the Group has undertaken initiatives to support the 
productive fabric in terms of access to credit and services. In this context, the product dedicated to olive-growing, called 
“Finanziamento Impiantolivo” with a direct Ismea guarantee was released in early July 2024 to finance farms that intend 
to build, restore or renovate olive-growing facilities and/or construct farm mills including bottling plants.   In addition, im-
portant memoranda were signed: 
• Memorandum of Understanding with Assocamerestero: the Joint Committee to set up the operational plan was establi-
shed, and regular meetings and operational sessions were organised to give impetus to the agreement;
• Memorandum of Understanding with the Ministry of Agriculture on food sovereignty and forestry;
• Memorandum of Understanding with the Region of Sicily - Department of Agriculture;
• Credit mediation agreement with Simec;
• Collaboration agreement with Coldiretti / CIB (Italian Biogas Consortium).
The Group has also adhered to the agreements signed between the Ministry of Agriculture, Food Sovereignty and Forestry 
(MASAF) and Cassa Depositi e Prestiti (CDP), concerning the financing of projects to support investments in the agri-food 
business. In particular, the Ministry signed agreements governing relations with authorities for the implementation and  
management of subsidised finance. Through these agreements, special Tenders (IV and V) were launched for “Supply 
Chain Agreements”, which through public and private financial support are expected to promote reorganisation proces -
ses in relations between operators in the Agri-food chain and Agri-energy chain. In 2024, loan extensions resolved in  
connection with the 4th Call for Proposals and new resolutions in connection with the 5th Call for Proposals totalled 198 
for about EUR 124 mln in total granted, while there were 47 stipulations concerning the 4th Call for Proposals in the year  
for about EUR 31 mln. Geographically, 68% of beneficiaries are situated in the South and supported by 41% of granted 
resources, while 18% of beneficiaries are located in central Italy, receiving 20% of contributions. Finally, the 15% of benefi-
ciaries in the North were financed with 39% of resources, in accordance with the table below:

title: Tourism
heading: 3.3.2.1.2.3.1 Tourism
start_phrase: To support businesses and development investments in tourism, the Group has signed up to the ABI, CDP and Ministry of Tourism Agreement to promote the Fondo Rotativo Imprese [Business Revolving Fund] with the aim of encouraging energy requalification, environmental sustainability and digital innovation in the tourism sector.
summary:
- Focus on the Group’s initiatives to support the productive economy—especially agriculture—through improved access to credit and services.
- Launch of “Finanziamento Impiantolivo” with a direct Ismea guarantee to finance olive grove development/restoration and construction or upgrading of mills and bottling plants.
- Series of strategic agreements: MoU with Assocamerestero (operational committee established), MoU with the Ministry of Agriculture on food sovereignty and forestry, MoU with the Sicily Region’s Department of Agriculture, a credit mediation agreement with Simec, and a collaboration with Coldiretti/CIB (Italian Biogas Consortium).
- Participation in MASAF–CDP frameworks supporting agri-food investments via Supply Chain Agreements (Tenders IV and V) aimed at reorganising agri-food and agri-energy chains; in 2024, 198 loan extensions/new resolutions totaling about EUR 124 million and 47 stipulations under the 4th Call for roughly EUR 31 million.
- Geographic allocation of beneficiaries and funds: South 68% of beneficiaries/41% of resources; Centre 18%/20%; North 15%/39%.
- Strengthening ties with protection consortia and producer organisations; in 2024, 23 new banking relationships with PDO/PGI consortia enabled around 1,900 member relationships.
- Community-support actions in tourism: adherence to the ABI–CDP–Ministry of Tourism agreement promoting the Fondo Rotativo Imprese for energy upgrades, environmental sustainability, and digital innovation; 11 projects financed in 2024 and 4 more in early 2025, for total investments exceeding EUR 41 million.
- Creation of the MPS Energia Verde business line to accelerate renewable energy adoption and energy autonomy for businesses and households, offering dedicated financial solutions, specialist advisory, partner networks, and support for accessing NRRP incentives.
text:
Tourism
To support businesses and development investments in tourism, the Group has signed up to the ABI, CDP and Ministry of 
Tourism Agreement to promote the Fondo Rotativo Imprese [Business Revolving Fund] with the aim of encouraging energy 
requalification, environmental sustainability and digital innovation in the tourism sector. The incentive is aimed at impro-
ving hospitality services and upgrading accommodation facilities in terms of digitisation and environmental sustainability 
(50% of funds are earmarked for energy upgrades). In 2024, 11 initiatives were financed and 4 more in the first 2 months 
of 2025 for a total investment of more than EUR 41 mln.

title: The Group and the support for green energy
heading: 3.3.2.1.2.3.2 The Group and the support for green energy
start_phrase: To encourage investments in production facilities or processes that, through the use of renewable sources, allow for the reduction of energy consumption or the pursuit of energy autonomy, the Group has activated a new business line with a specific brand, MPS Energia Verde, with which it intends to support businesses and families in their transition process, making dedicated and flexible products and solutions available to customers, as well as specialist consultancy and a network with specialised partners.
summary:
- Focus area: How the Group supports local communities and sectors through credit access, partnerships, energy transition, tourism development, and cultural heritage stewardship, within its sustainability agenda.

- Agriculture and agri-food support:
  - Launched “Finanziamento Impiantolivo” with direct Ismea guarantee to finance olive-growing facilities, mills, and bottling plants.
  - Signed key agreements: Assocamerestero (operational plan via Joint Committee), Ministry of Agriculture (food sovereignty and forestry), Region of Sicily (Dept. of Agriculture), Simec (credit mediation), Coldiretti/CIB (biogas).
  - Adhered to MASAF–CDP frameworks for subsidised finance, activating Tenders IV and V for Supply Chain Agreements to reorganise agri-food and agri-energy chains.
  - 2024 results: 198 loan extensions/new resolutions for about EUR 124 million; 47 stipulations on the 4th Call for about EUR 31 million.
  - Geographic allocation: South 68% of beneficiaries/41% of resources; Centre 18%/20%; North 15%/39%.
  - Expanded ties with protection consortia and producer organisations: 23 new bank relationships with PDO/PGI consortia, enabling roughly 1,900 member relationships.

- Tourism sector initiatives:
  - Joined ABI–CDP–Ministry of Tourism agreement promoting the Fondo Rotativo Imprese to improve hospitality via energy requalification, environmental sustainability, and digital innovation (50% of funds earmarked for energy upgrades).
  - Financed 11 initiatives in 2024 and 4 more in early 2025, totaling over EUR 41 million in investment.

- Green energy and energy transition:
  - Launched MPS Energia Verde to support businesses and households with dedicated products, specialist consultancy, and partner networks.
  - Supports access to NRRP incentives, including: Transition 5.0, Renewable Energy Communities (CER), agrivoltaics, biomethane, and self-production.
  - Opened 15 MPS Energia Verde centers across Italy with specialised staff and sector/academic partnerships.

- Art, culture, and heritage:
  - Strategy to conserve and enhance the Group’s historical and artistic assets (art collections and Historical Archive) while enabling public access.
  - Conservation in 2024: oversight and security monitoring; restoration of 139 artefacts (110 paintings, 24 sculptures, 5 ceramic/bronze plates) by accredited restorers.
  - Cultural engagement: participation in ABI’s Cultural Relations working group; free-use agreements with cultural institutions; loans of 130+ works for 12 exhibitions in Italy and abroad; 20 consultations of the Historical Archive.
  - Renewed free use with Casa Buonarroti Foundation and Municipality of Casole d’Elsa; loaned 2,184 Gonzaga coins/medals to Palazzo Ducale di Mantua for display.
  - The Historical Archive is officially recognized as a Private Archive of notable historical interest.

- Objectives and monitoring:
  - No specific measurable targets yet for affected communities; ongoing monitoring via initiative-based indicators (e.g., internships, career day participation under MPS Orienta).
  - Commitment to evaluate and adopt specific targets in the future for continuous improvement.
text:
The Group and the support for green energy 
To encourage investments in production facilities or processes that, through the use of renewable sources, allow for the  
reduction of energy consumption or the pursuit of energy autonomy, the Group has activated a new business line with a spe-
cific brand, MPS Energia Verde, with which it intends to support businesses and families in their transition process, making  
dedicated and flexible products and solutions available to customers, as well as specialist consultancy and a network 
with specialised partners. In particular, the Group intends to encourage the construction of energy production plants from 
renewable sources, with the support of specialists able to provide detailed advice on the functioning of the measures  
to support the energy supply chain, including through customer support aimed at accessing the incentives provided by  
the NRRP , especially with regard to:BANCA MONTE DEI PASCHI DI SIENA218• Transition 5.0, which supports the digital and energy transformation process of companies;
• CER, which stimulates the creation and development of Renewable Energy Communities;
• Agrivoltaic, which promotes hybrid agriculture-energy systems through non-repayable grants and incentive tariffs  
for electricity fed into the grid;
• Biomethane, which supports investments to build new biomethane production plants and for the total or partial  
reconversion of existing biogas plants powered by agricultural or agro-industrial biomass;
• Support for self-production, to encourage the self-production of energy from renewable sources in Italy;
The initiative involved the opening of 15 MPS Energia Verde centers located throughout Italy, where specialized resources 
operate who have access to a network of contacts with associations and experts in the sector, also coming from the aca-
demic world.

title: Art and culture for the Group
heading: 3.3.2.1.2.3.3 Art and culture for the Group
start_phrase: The strategies adopted are also aimed at promoting cultural initiatives as an element of the Group’s identity.
summary:
- Focus on supporting Italy’s energy transition through dedicated financing and advisory for:
  - Transition 5.0 (digital and energy transformation of companies)
  - Renewable Energy Communities (CER)
  - Agrivoltaics (grants and incentive tariffs for hybrid agriculture–energy systems)
  - Biomethane (new plants and reconversion of biogas facilities)
  - Self-production of renewable energy
- Launch of 15 MPS Energia Verde centers across Italy staffed by specialists with networks spanning associations, sector experts, and academia.
- Strong commitment to art and culture as part of Group identity:
  - Conservation and enhancement of the Group’s historical and artistic heritage, including its art collection and Historical Archive.
  - Continuous monitoring of conservation and security; annual maintenance/restoration in coordination with Superintendence Offices.
  - In 2024, restoration on 139 artefacts (110 paintings, 24 sculptures, 5 ceramic/bronze plates) by certified professional restorers (per Italian Legislative Decree 42/2004, Art. 182).
- Sector collaboration and public access:
  - Participation in ABI’s Cultural Relations working group to align cultural strategies across banks.
  - Ensured consultation access to book and archival materials.
  - Expanded public enjoyment through free-use agreements with cultural institutions.
  - In 2024: over 130 artworks lent to 12 temporary exhibitions in Italy and abroad; 20 research consultations at the Historical Archive.
  - Renewed free-use of works with the Casa Buonarroti Foundation (Florence) and Municipality of Casole d’Elsa.
  - New free-loan to Palazzo Ducale di Mantua of the Gonzaga coin and medal collection (2,184 items) for exhibition, enhancing local cultural value.
- Objectives and monitoring:
  - No specific measurable targets yet for impacts on affected communities; ongoing monitoring via initiative-linked indicators (e.g., MPS Orienta tracks internships and career day participation).
  - Future evaluation of setting specific targets to strengthen community impact management.
- Note: The Bank’s Historical Archive is officially recognized as a Private Archive of notable historical interest by the Ministry of Cultural and Environmental Heritage (deed no. 685, 7 April 1997), with corresponding preservation obligations.
text:
Art and culture for the Group
The strategies adopted are also aimed at promoting cultural initiatives as an element of the Group’s identity. In 2024, the 
main lines of action in this area concerned the conservation and enhancement of the Group’s historical and artistic heritage  
in order to meet two fundamental needs: conserve assets for future generations and promote cultural enjoyment and 
the dissemination of knowledge. Activities related to policies to enhance heritage are developed in a manner compatible  
with protection, without compromising conservation requirements. The Group’s heritage, which has stratified over time, 
consists of the art collection, divided into various collection nuclei, and the Historical Archive47.
As regards conservation and restoration, the Group ensures careful, constant oversight of the works in the collection, 
regularly monitoring their conservation conditions, as well as security aspects - to prevent possible risks of damage and 
maintain their integrity. In addition, maintenance and restoration work is carried out annually on items that require specific 
attention. This work is planned in agreement with local Superintendence Offices for the Fine Arts. During the year, work 
was carried out on 139 artefacts, including 110 paintings, 24 sculptures and 5 ceramic and bronze plates. The restorers 
were selected from the List of Professional Restorers of Cultural Heritage pursuant to Article 182, Italian Legislative Decree 
42/2004, depending on the kind of asset being restored.
The Group, through its participation in the Cultural Relations working group of the Italian Banking Association (ABI),  
identifies the cultural strategies to be pursued, shared by all banking institutions. In this context, the Group ensures that 
book and archive materials can be consulted. In addition, in order to promote public enjoyment, free usage contracts have 
been signed with cultural bodies and institutions, which allow for a wider opening to the community through projects that 
enrich the local and national cultural offering. In 2024, more than 130 works of art were lent as part of 12 temporary exhi-
bitions in Italy and abroad. As for consultations for study and research activities, in 2024 there were 20 accesses to the 
Historical Archive.
Free use of the works was also renewed at the Casa Buonarroti Foundation, Florence, and the Municipality of Casole 
d’Elsa. During the year, a free loan agreement was entered into with the Museum Complex of Palazzo Ducale di Mantua,  
concerning the Gonzaga collection of coins and medals (consisting of 2,184 items), for exhibition purposes in the Rustica 
rooms of Palazzo Ducale, to bring greater value to the local area.

Objectives 
The Group has not currently defined specific measurable objectives to manage the issue that has been found to be material  
with reference to the affected communities, but it does monitor the policies and actions in relation to the impacts on

title: Processes for engaging with affected communities about impacts
heading: 3.3.3 Processes for engaging with affected communities about impacts
start_phrase: The Group’s business model seeks to enhance the needs of customers and small and medium-sized enterprises rooted in the territory by listening to their needs in order to identify new opportunities and community needs.
summary:
- Focus on engaging affected communities to understand impacts, identify local needs, and share the Group’s artistic heritage and knowledge, with emphasis on customers and SMEs rooted in the territory.
- Use of events and sponsorships to foster transparent, participatory relationships with local stakeholders.
- A formal, regulated communication framework governed by the Group Communication and External Relations Directive to ensure consistency and clarity.
- External communication overseen by the External Communication, Institutional Relations Department, which:
  - Defines policies, criteria, rules, and plans communication initiatives.
  - Implements or monitors communication activities across Group companies.
  - Plans and organizes conferences, seminars, openings, exhibitions, and fairs.
- The “Media Relations, Events and Sponsoring” function coordinates delegated activities and requires Group functions to report engagement initiatives from proposal/awareness to enable accurate assessment.
- Commitment to supporting vulnerable and marginalized communities through listening programs, youth employability initiatives, and backing for strategic sectors such as agribusiness and tourism.
- Broader commitment to community rights and sustainable development that creates value for stakeholders and enhances local economic and social well-being.
- Concrete actions include:
  - Contributions to cultural, scientific, social, and environmental initiatives.
  - Work orientation and financial education programs.
  - Products and services tailored for vulnerable groups.
  - Partnerships with local institutions to advance sustainable supply chains and social health and well-being.
- Governance anchored in the Group’s Code of Ethics, ensuring compliance with internal procedures, external codes and international agreements, and legal/regulatory obligations, with principles applied to activities involving local areas, the environment, and the community.
text:
Processes for engaging with affected communities about impacts
The Group’s business model seeks to enhance the needs of customers and small and medium-sized enterprises rooted in 
the territory by listening to their needs in order to identify new opportunities and community needs. The Group recognises  
the importance of the point of view of the affected communities, promoting structured interaction with associations,  
bodies, institutions and players in the civil economy, operating in the area. In particular, through dialogue with the commu -
nity and territories, the Group seeks to share its artistic heritage and knowledge. 
The focus on communication with and involvement of the target communities is directly implemented through events  
and sponsorships as tools for dialogue and discussion with stakeholders. Through such initiatives, the institute aims  
to forge solid and transparent relationships, encouraging the participation and involvement of all local stakeholders. 
This commitment translates into a regulated and formalised approach, seeking consistency and clarity in communication  
activities, governed by the Group Communication and External Relations Directive. In particular, the Group’s external  
communication is overseen by the External Communication, Institutional Relations Department, through:
• the definition of policies, criteria, rules and the planning of communication initiativ e (opportunities, priorities, etc.);
• the direct implementation of communication initiatives or the monitoring and control of measures implemented directly 
by Group companies within the limits of granted powers;
• the planning and holding of conferences (congresses, seminars, openings) and exhibitions and fairs. 
In addition, the “Media Relations, Events and Sponsoring” function coordinates and supervises any activities delegated to 
the relevant Group functions. In particular, the functions of the Group companies involved in the conception and/or planning 
of an engagement initiative are required to report the related data of the intervention itself to the above-mentioned function.  
This reporting must be carried out from the time when the initiative is proposed and, for events planned by external  
parties, from the time when they become aware of it, in order to allow for an accurate assessment of the initiative by the 
Functions in charge of this area.
The Group is also committed to supporting the most vulnerable and marginalised communities, through specific actions 
to listen and respond to their needs. Through support programmes, the Group stimulates youth employability and supports 
strategic sectors such as agribusiness and tourism.

title: The Group’s commitment to community rights
heading: 3.3.4 The Group’s commitment to community rights
start_phrase: The Group pursues the creation of value for all significant stakeholders through a sustainable development model aimed at the growth of its customers and the territory in which it operates.
summary:
- Focus on how the Group engages affected communities to understand and address impacts, emphasizing listening, local roots, and sharing cultural/artistic heritage.
- Use of events and sponsorships to foster dialogue, transparency, and participation among local stakeholders.
- Formal governance of external communication through the Group Communication and External Relations Directive, led by the External Communication, Institutional Relations Department.
- Departmental responsibilities include setting policies and criteria, planning communication initiatives, overseeing or executing activities across Group companies, and organizing conferences, exhibitions, and fairs.
- “Media Relations, Events and Sponsoring” coordinates and supervises delegated engagement activities; Group functions must report proposed initiatives early (including third-party events once known) for centralized assessment.
- Commitment to support vulnerable and marginalized communities via listening initiatives, youth employability programs, and support for strategic sectors such as agribusiness and tourism.
- Community rights and social value creation pursued through contributions to cultural, scientific, social, and environmental initiatives; work orientation and financial education; tailored products/services for vulnerable groups; and partnerships with local institutions for sustainable supply chains, wellbeing, and health.
- Ethical foundation anchored in the Group’s Code of Ethics, aligning with internal rules, external codes, international commitments, and legal requirements across geographies; principles apply to activities impacting local areas, environment, and community.
- ESRS S4 Consumers and end-users: double materiality assessment covering impacts, risks, opportunities, policies, actions, targets, engagement processes, and remedy/concern-raising channels.
- Identified impacts, risks, opportunities:
  - Negative impacts (Own Operations and Downstream): potential inadequacy of customer/end-user data protection safeguards.
  - Positive impacts (Own Operations): practices ensuring freedom of expression (e.g., complaint channels), clear and transparent access to products/services, personal safety, and social inclusion, supported by digitalization (e.g., improved authentication, inclusive technologies).
  - Risks (Own Operations and Downstream): operational and reputational risks from potential personal data breaches.
  - Opportunities (Own Operations and Downstream): strengthen stakeholder trust via robust privacy and expression safeguards; expand inclusive products and services and enhance privacy protections.
- Scope of stakeholders considered includes institutional, corporate, and retail customers, as well as business partners and suppliers; mapping drew on internal policies, public documents, and customer-protection initiatives (e.g., digital communications, digital banking).
text:
The Group pursues the creation of value for all significant stakeholders through a sustainable development model aimed 
at the growth of its customers and the territory in which it operates.
The Group seeks the promotion, development of economic well-being and the quality of the social contexts in which it 
operates by supporting programmes to protect communities and territories. More specifically, we report:
• contributions to cultural, scientific, social and environmental initiatives;
• work orientation and financial education activities;
• products and services for the most vulnerable and needy groups and individuals in society;
• partnerships with local institutions for the sustainable growth of the production chain, and for the development 
• of wellbeing and the health of the social context.
The reference policy is the Group’s Code of Ethics, which set forth the commitment to comply with internal rules and pro-
cedures, external codes and agreements, including international ones, to which it adheres, contractual provisions and legal 
and regulatory obligations in force in every geographical context and sphere of activity in which it operates.
The principles of the Code apply to the Group’s activities and concern all actions dedicated to local areas, the environment 
and the community. For further details on the Code of Ethics and alignment with international standards and initiatives, see 
the “Business conduct” chapter of “Section 4 - Information on Go vernance”. BANCA MONTE DEI PASCHI DI SIENA220

title: Impacts, Risks and Opportunities
heading: 3.4.1 Impacts, Risks and Opportunities
start_phrase: The process to map impacts, risks and opportunities with reference to this standard includes the specific aspects related to the Group’s operational and commercial activities.
summary:
- Focus: ESRS S4 Consumers and end-users for Banca Monte dei Paschi di Siena, covering double materiality (impacts, risks, opportunities), policies, actions, targets, stakeholder engagement, grievance/remedy channels.
- Stakeholders in scope: institutional, corporate, and retail customers, along with business partners and suppliers (as end-users of products/services).
- Key impact areas: data protection and privacy, accessibility and inclusion in financial services, quality and transparency of information, freedom of expression, personal safety, non-discrimination, and responsible business practices.
- Material impacts and scope:
  - Negative: potential inadequacy of safeguards for customer/end-user information (Own Operations and Downstream Value Chain).
  - Positive: business practices supporting freedom of expression (e.g., complaint mechanisms), clear and transparent product information, personal safety, social inclusion, and process digitalisation (e.g., enhanced user authentication) within Own Operations.
- Risks: operational and reputational risks from potential personal data protection violations across Own Operations and Downstream Value Chain.
- Opportunities: strengthen stakeholder trust via robust privacy and expression safeguards (Own Operations); expand inclusive products/services and enhance privacy protections (Downstream Value Chain).
- Sub-topics mapped under S4: privacy, freedom of expression, access to quality information, health and safety, non-discrimination, access to products and services, responsible business practices; assessed for impact and financial materiality across own operations, upstream, and downstream.
- Privacy and IT security governance:
  - Data Protection Policy: defines privacy controls by design/by default, data subject rights, processing records, data breach management, roles/responsibilities, information flows, planning/reporting, and employee training. Approved by Board of Directors; applies to Parent Company, Widiba, and fiduciary entities; aligned with GDPR, Italian Privacy Code, EDPB guidance; public on the Group website.
  - Group Policy on Logical Security Governance: establishes the Information Security Management System (ISMS), roles, and responsibilities; centralized governance by the Parent Company’s Information Security function; implementation with IT; aligned with ISO/IEC 2700x; available on intranet; applies to all Group companies.
- ISMS approach: lifecycle protection of data and information, risk assessment, and preventive/protective measures to meet regulatory and asset protection requirements.
- Next sections (not fully shown): actions and targets for privacy, customer listening and complaint handling, product information quality, personal safety, non-discrimination, accessibility (including digitalisation), and responsible business practices.
text:
The process to map impacts, risks and opportunities with reference to this standard includes the specific aspects related 
to the Group’s operational and commercial activities. As a financial institution, the Group offers a wide range of financial 
products and services that could impact consumers and end-users as customers. These impacts relate, for example,  
to the issues of data protection, accessibility of financial services and inclusion. Interaction with customers and end-users 
of our products and services may, on the other hand, also entail risks, such as risks related to the potential breach of infor-
mation systems resulting in the loss of sensitive data and reputational impacts. Finally, this interaction can also generate 
opportunities for the Group, e.g. by increasing customer confidence in the safeguards defined to protect customers.
The mapping process included the analysis of the Group’s internal policies, public documentation, the identification of the 
initiatives taken to protect customers and end-users (e.g. digitalised communications to customers and Digital Banking  
operations) with reference to all categories of customers and end-users that could be materially impacted by the Group. 
In particular, customers and end users include institutional, corporate and retail customers of the Group’s products  
and services as well as business partners and suppliers.
On the basis of the analyses performed, the following were material: 
• Negative impacts with reference to the Own Operations  and Downstream Value Chain perimeter related to the potential 
inadequacy of safeguards to protect information concerning customers and end users;
• Positive impacts  pertaining to the Own Operations  perimeter related to the existence of business practices and  
strategies aimed at safeguarding customers’ freedom of expression, access to products and services presented in a 
clear and transparent manner, personal safety and social inclusion. Examples include initiatives aimed at digitalising 
processes (e.g. user authentication methods to improve the customer experience, the adoption of technological solu -
tions products aimed at social inclusion);
• Operational and reputational risk related to the Own Operations  and Downstream Value Chain perimeter and linked to 
the potential violation of personal data protection of customers and end users; 
• Opportunities  related to the Own Operations perimeter attributable to the increase of Stakeholder confidence in the defi-
nition and implementation of safeguards to ensure freedom of expression (e.g. through the submission of complaints) 
and the protection of customers’ personal data. With regard to the Downstream Value Chain, opportunities can be found 
in the expansion of the range of products and services aimed at ensuring the social inclusion of customers and the 
strengthening of privacy safeguards.2024 ANNUAL REPORT - Sustainability Reporting 221Topic Sub-Topic/

title: Policies
heading: 3.4.2.1.1 Policies
start_phrase: In the context of customer and end-user protection, privacy protection and IT security safeguards play a key role in ensuring that data and information, throughout their entire lifecycle, are adequately protected, in accordance with regulatory requirements on the protection of personal data and safeguarding of company assets.
summary:
- Focus: Customer and end‑user privacy and IT security, ensuring protection of personal data and information assets throughout their lifecycle in line with regulatory requirements.

- Key policies:
  - Data Protection Policy: Defines privacy controls (privacy by design/by default), data subject rights management, records of processing, data breach management, roles/responsibilities, information flows, planning/reporting, and employee training. Scope: Parent Company, Widiba Group, Fiduciaria companies. Governance: Approved and overseen by the Board. Compliance: GDPR, Italian Privacy Code, guidance from the Italian DPA/EDPB. Availability: Group website (Sustainability section).
  - Group Policy on Logical Security Governance: Establishes the Information Security Management System (ISMS), organizational model, principles, and responsibilities for logical security across all Group companies. Centralized governance by the Parent Company’s Information Security function; implementation with Information Security and IT. Aligns with ISO/IEC 2700x. Availability: Corporate intranet.

- ISMS approach and coverage:
  - Risk‑based management of security across ICT service lifecycle; integrated into all processes and channels across the Group.
  - Objectives: Confidentiality, integrity, availability, verifiability, accountability.
  - Activities: Define security architecture and requirements; incident management; fraud prevention; emergency communications; change management; monitoring, audit facilitation, and continuous improvement.
  - Staff awareness and training are central to effectiveness.

- Review cadence: Directive reviewed annually and updated at least every three years or upon significant changes (laws, standards, internal/outsourced processes, threat landscape, technologies, organization).

- Actions completed in 2022–2024:
  - Firewall configuration review to align with international frameworks, remove non‑compliant rules, and enforce updated standards.
  - “Zero password” initiative introducing passwordless customer authentication (e.g., push notifications, biometrics).

- Ongoing initiatives: Regular employee training programs on information security, with needs identified via the 3D approach model.

In the context of customer and end-user protection, privacy protection and IT security safeguards play a key role in ensu -
ring that data and information, throughout their entire lifecycle, are adequately protected, in accordance with regulatory 
requirements on the protection of personal data and safeguarding of company assets. 
The Group implements policies on this issue through the ‘Data Protection Policy’ and the ‘Group Policy on Logical Security  
Governance’, which define the guidelines and objectives to be pursued, through the ‘Information Security Management 
System’ (hereafter ISMS). to ensure that data and information, during their entire life cycle, are adequately protected,  
in accordance with regulatory requirements on the protection of personal data and the safeguarding of company assets. 
The ISMS is based on the assessment of all risks associated with the subject and their management through the  
planning and implementation of the prevention and protection measures necessary to minimise these risks. 2024 ANNUAL REPORT - Sustainability Reporting 223To guarantee the reliability of the information processed, as well as the effectiveness and efficiency of the processes  
involving the Group’s stakeholders (customers, shareholders, suppliers, partners, etc.), all security aspects must be properly  
taken into account and integrated into all phases of the ICT service life cycle and apply to all forms of personal data,  
regardless of the data subject to whom they refer and/or the channel through which they are received, and apply to all 
Group companies. The above said Directive is reviewed annually and updated at least every three years, or in any case whe-
never a significant change is detected in reference legislation, security standards, internal processes, processes adopted 
by outsourcers, attack scenarios, Group technologies and organisational structure is detected.
