heading: 3.4.5 Protecting the human rights of consumers and end users
start_phrase: In line with the significance identified in the Double Materiality Analysis of issues related to consumers and end users, the Group is committed to developing relationships of trust and mutual and lasting satisfaction with customers, marked by va- lues of transparency and fairness.
summary:
- Describes the Group’s complaints and mediation framework, noting no formal stakeholder involvement in procedure design or review, but systematic tracking of effectiveness via customer complaints, appeals (ABF/ACF), complaint reiterations, and outcomes as proxies for satisfaction.
- Details quantitative and qualitative monitoring of the Complaints and Mediation Department, including adherence to processing times and effectiveness metrics (upheld/partially upheld/rejected complaints, and arbitration decisions by outcome).
- Confirms annual public reporting on complaint handling in line with the Bank of Italy’s Supervisory Provisions on transparency and fairness, and highlights the department’s organizational independence from marketing to avoid conflicts of interest.
- Outlines Banca Widiba’s specific grievance-handling pathway: initial recourse to Customer Care via Mediacenter or the customer’s advisor; if unresolved, formal written complaints via mail, email (reclami@widipec.it), or delivery through the advisor, with required contents (identification, relationship details, contact, issue description, supporting documents).
- Introduces the “Complaints Register” to standardize complaint management with Group procedures, enable early resolution, classify cases per ABI standards, and ensure ongoing monitoring.
- Defines what constitutes a complaint, including verbal objections on services/contractual relations, written objections via web channels (chat, social media), and clarification requests from journalists/newspapers.
- Sets out commitments to protect the human rights of consumers and end users: transparency, fairness, compliance with internal/external rules and laws, counterparty due diligence to avoid links to illegal or harmful activities, and adherence to the UN Global Compact and UNEP Principles for Responsible Banking.
- Specifies minimum sustainability criteria and exclusions: no financing where evidence of human rights or labor violations, fraud, money laundering, corruption, terrorism financing, or involvement with controversial/internationally banned weapons; no support for transactions involving sanctioned/embargoed countries, armed conflict contexts, or governments committing serious human rights violations.
- Introduces Governance Information – Business Conduct (ESRS G1): scope includes impacts, risks, opportunities; preventive/mitigative policies and actions; targets and metrics to assess effectiveness.
- Highlights governance mechanisms: a Board-approved Code of Ethics integrated with the 231 Compliance Programme; dissemination to subsidiaries/partners; monitoring via internal controls; and the presence on governing bodies of members with specialized expertise in business conduct and Legislative Decree 231/2001.
- Summarizes impacts, risks, and opportunities: strong safeguards for corporate culture, whistleblower protection, and anti-corruption training; recognition of evolving risks (e.g., IT security breaches); potential opportunities (enhanced stakeholder trust); and material positive impacts from practices that foster culture, protect whistleblowers, and prevent corruption.
text:
Protecting the human rights of consumers and end users
In line with the significance identified in the Double Materiality Analysis of issues related to consumers and end users, the 
Group is committed to developing relationships of trust and mutual and lasting satisfaction with customers, marked by va-
lues of transparency and fairness. The Group has therefore put policies and processes in place to promote the protection 
of human rights and to follow a conduct inspired by integrity and respect, committing to:
• complying with internal rules and procedures, the external codes and agreements, both national and international, to 
which it adheres, contractual provisions and legal and regulatory obligations in force in each geographical context and 
sphere of activity where it operates;BANCA MONTE DEI PASCHI DI SIENA242• assessing the seriousness and reliability of organisations it has a direct or indirect relationship with, paying attention 
to their possible involvement in activities that are illegal, harmful to human rights, or detrimental to human health and 
safety; 
• operating in line with the principles of the UN Global Compact and the UNEP Principles for Responsible Banking which 
it endorses;
• complying with the minimum sustainability criteria identified by the Group as mandatory, consistent with the relevant 
international, European and national (conventions that apply to all counterparties and projects, in order not to provide 
funding to counterparties and projects for which, during the assessment, evidence will emerge of adverse impacts 
and of legal proceedings relating to violations of human rights (including health and safety standards), violations of 
fundamental labour rights and child and forced labour standards, financial and non-financial reporting fraud, money 
laundering, corruption or financing of terrorism, and which involve controversial and/or internationally banned weapons 
(e.g. nuclear, biological and chemical weapons, cluster bombs, weapons containing depleted uranium, anti-personnel 
landmines). The Group does not support transactions destined for countries subject to sanctions and embargoes, coun -
tries in armed conflict and/or whose governments have been responsible for serious violations of international human 
rights conventions, nor does it have relations with entities operating in these market sectors.2024 ANNUAL REPORT - Sustainability Reporting 243

start_phrase: The Group adopts a Code of Ethics that forms the basis of its activities.
summary:
- Context: ESRS G1 Business Conduct section of the Sustainability Report’s Governance chapter, outlining impacts, risks, opportunities, policies, actions, targets, and metrics related to managing ethical business conduct.
- Governance framework: Adoption of a Board-approved Code of Ethics and a 231 Compliance Programme as core governance tools; binding for directors, auditors, managers, employees, and promoted to affiliates, partners, consultants, and external staff; compliance assessed in relationships and monitored via the internal control system.
- Board expertise: In 2024, boards include members with specialized knowledge and experience in business conduct and administrative liability under Legislative Decree 231/2001, gained through supervisory roles, directorships/auditor positions, academic lecturing, participation in ethical associations and study groups, economic crime consulting, and legal scholarship.
- Impacts, risks, and opportunities mapping: Based on analysis of operational/commercial activities and governance documents; highlights initiatives to protect customers and end consumers, including anti-corruption training, whistleblowing mechanisms, and the 231 Management Model.
- Safeguards: Strong measures to uphold corporate culture, protect whistleblowers, and prevent active and passive corruption.
- Risks: Potential breaches of the Group’s IT security amid a changing environment.
- Opportunities: Increased stakeholder confidence stemming from robust whistleblower protections.
- Materiality outcome (Own Operations): Positive impacts identified from adopting corporate practices and policies that disseminate a sound corporate culture, ensure whistleblower protection, and prevent corruption through training.
text:
The Group adopts a Code of Ethics that forms the basis of its activities. It is approved by the Board of Directors in the 
same way as the Bank’s Compliance Programme (231 Model) and it sets out the guiding principles, the values and rules 
of conduct (in addition to legal and regulatory obligations), which the directors, auditors, managers and employees of the 
Group companies undertake to respect and disseminate in the performance of their duties, in relation to their respective 
responsibilities.
The Group also undertakes to promote the dissemination of the principles of the Code of Ethics to associated compa-
nies, subsidiaries, investees, business partners, consultants and external staff and associates. Compliance with the code  
is evaluated in current and future relations. The Code of Ethics is therefore a governance tool and an integral part of the 
231 Compliance Programme, binding on all those involved. Its implementation is monitored and verified under the internal 
control system.
In addition, the presence in the Board of Directors and the Board of Statutory Auditors, in the year 2024, of members with 
specific theoretical knowledge and practical experience on the subject of business conduct, with a focus on administrative 
liability pursuant to Legislative Decree No. 231/2001, acquired and matured through: 
• role as member of Supervisory Bodies pursuant to Legislative Decree 231, including in listed companies and banks; 
• experience as director and/or statutory auditor of listed companies and banks;
• Lecturer in Master’s Course on administrative liability of entities; 
• membership of associations/organisations/independent bodies with an ethical purpose and membership of study 
groups on administrative liability of entities;
• consulting on economic crime;
• Legal knowledge deriving from studies in law, the practice of law and/or academia, and the publication of scholarly 
articles.

  - Safeguards in place for corporate culture, whistleblower protection and anti-corruption; acknowledgment of evolving IT security risks; opportunity to build stakeholder trust via robust whistleblower protections.
  - Double materiality outcomes (Own Operations focus):
    - Positive impacts: stronger corporate culture, whistleblower protection, anti-corruption training.
    - Negative impacts: potential inadequacy of cybersecurity safeguards affecting IT/network system security for customers.
    - Risks: reputational risk from weak cybersecurity; risks from employee breaches of customer privacy/information.

- Policies, actions and targets on business conduct (corporate culture focus):

The process of mapping impacts, risks and opportunities with reference to the standard in question is based on the analysis  
of the specific aspects associated with the Group’s operational and commercial activities, its strategic and governance 
documentation, both internal and public, and the identification of the initiatives selected and adopted to protect customers 
and end consumers (e.g. ongoing training on anti-corruption issues, whistleblowing and the 231 Management Model).  
In fact, the Group has put in place strong safeguards to define and ensure compliance with the principles relating to 
corporate culture, to protect whistleblowers and to prevent active and passive corruption. The changing environment 
could also entail risks for the financial institution, such as risks related to the potential breach of the Group’s IT security.  
Finally, this interaction can also generate opportunities for the Group, e.g. by increasing stakeholder confidence in the 
safeguards defined to protect whistleblowers.
After conducting the double materiality assessment, the following aspects were found to be material with reference  
to Own Operations:
• Positive impacts: related to the adoption of corporate practices and policies aimed at disseminating a mindful and 
adequate corporate culture within the Group, ensuring the protection of whistleblowers and preventing corruption 
through training;BANCA MONTE DEI PASCHI DI SIENA244• Negative impact: connected to the lack of adequate safeguards to ensure the security of the Group IT and network 
systems for the benefit of customers through the implementation of cybersecurity policies and safeguards;
• Risks:  related to Reputational Risk  arising from possible inadequate cybersecurity safeguards aimed at ensuring  
the security of IT and network systems for the benefit of the Group customers and stakeholders, and from breaches  
of customer privacy/information by employees;
• Opportunities:  increased stakeholder confidence related to whistleblower protection.

heading: 4.1.3.1 Policies
start_phrase: Material Group policies on corporate culture include the Group’s Code of Ethics and the Group Policy on Governance Security Logic.
summary:
- Focus area: G1 Conduct of Enterprises in the Sustainability Report, covering corporate culture, whistleblower protection, anti- and active/passive corruption (with links to cybersecurity), and connections to AML/CFT.
- Materiality highlights:
  - Negative impacts: potential lack of adequate cybersecurity safeguards for Group IT and network systems.
  - Risks: reputational risk from inadequate cybersecurity and potential breaches of customer privacy/information by employees.
  - Opportunities: stronger stakeholder confidence through effective whistleblower protection.
  - Scope: considerations span own operations and the upstream/downstream value chain; outcomes addressed for both impact and financial materiality.
- Corporate culture policies:
  - Code of Ethics: sets principles, values, and conduct rules for internal and external relations, supports sustainability objectives, and aligns Group goals with societal interests.
  - Governance and oversight: Code is part of Model 231, approved by the Board; compliance and internal audit manage confidential reporting, assessment, and escalation to corporate bodies and the 231 Supervisory Board.
  - Applicability and standards: applies Group-wide across geographies and stakeholders; aligned with internal rules, external codes/agreements, and legal/regulatory obligations; publicly available on the corporate website.
- Cybersecurity framework:
  - Strategic stance: IT security as a core cultural pillar to ensure resilience, robustness, and responsiveness.
  - Policy/Directive on Logical Security Governance: establishes the Information Security Management System (ISMS) to protect information across its lifecycle; defines organizational model, principles, roles, and long-term direction.
  - Governance model: centralized at the Parent Company’s Information Security function; implemented by Group companies via top-management resolutions; supported by Information Security and IT functions.
  - Standards and transparency: ISMS managed in line with internal/external standards, notably ISO/IEC 2700x series; overview available on the corporate website.
- The section introduces the Group’s Policies, Actions, and Targets related to whistleblower protection, prevention of corruption, and cybersecurity safeguards.
text:
Policies
Material Group policies on corporate culture include the Group’s Code of Ethics and the Group Policy on Governance  
Security Logic.
Code of Ethics
The Group’s Code of Ethics contains the principles, values and rules of conduct  that the Group is committed to following 
in all its activities, in its internal relations, in its relations with the market and significant stakeholders, and with the  
environment.  
The Code is an essential part of Model 231 (the Organisation, Management and Control Model for the prevention of offences  
pursuant to Legislative Decree 231/01) as it supplements the model in terms of expressing and communicating values, 
principles and rules of conduct.
Any non-compliance and conduct considered not in line with the provisions of the Code can also be detected by each 
corporate function, as part of control activities pertinent to their own spheres of responsibility. Relevant reports are 
to be sent at the same time to the Compliance and Internal Audit Functions through the formal reporting procedure.  
They must be treated confidentially and analysed to assess their relevance, taking corrective and/or improvement action 
if necessary. To this end, the compliance function examines the reports for the aspects within its competence, also  
nforming the internal audit function, which, through auditing activities, assesses and ascertains possible conduct that  
suggests a breach of the Code, and presents the results to the relevant corporate bodies and to the 231 Supervisory Board 
(hereinafter also referred to as 231 SB).
In defining the contents of the policies, the Group gives due consideration to the interests of key stakeholders, as detailed 
in the Stakeholder Engagement process section of this document.2024 ANNUAL REPORT - Sustainability Reporting 245Policies Description

heading: 4.1.3.2 Cybersecurity
start_phrase: IT security is one of the fundamental pillars of the Group’s culture, which is committed to ensuring the resilience, robustness and responsiveness of its digital system.
summary:
- Focus of the section: Governance policies and actions within the Group’s Sustainability Reporting, centered on the Code of Ethics and Cybersecurity/Logical Security Governance, plus related training and implementation measures.
- Code of Ethics:
  - Objectives: define standards of good conduct; inform employees of required behavior; support implementation of Group sustainability policies; align Group objectives with civil society interests.
  - Scope: addressed to the entire corporate population across all geographies and value chain stages; stated as applicable to all customers.
  - Governance and validation: approved by the Bank’s Board of Directors; implementation ensured via the internal control system.
  - Commitments and references: adherence to internal rules and procedures; external codes and agreements (including international); contractual, legal, and regulatory obligations in each operating context.
  - Availability: published in the Sustainability section of the corporate website.
- Cybersecurity and Logical Security Governance:
  - IT security positioned as a fundamental pillar to ensure resilience, robustness, and responsiveness of digital systems.
  - Group Directive/Policy defines and implements an Information Security Management System (ISMS) to protect data and information across their lifecycle and all company activities.
  - Group Policy on Logical Security Governance:
    - Defines organizational model, principles, and responsibilities for Logical Security Governance and sets a medium/long-term strategic direction.
    - Scope: applies to the Parent Company and all Group companies.
    - Validation and implementation: adopted by Group companies through top management resolutions, with adaptation to company size/characteristics; governance centralized in the Parent Company’s Information Security function; implementation guided by Information Security and IT functions.
    - Standards: managed in line with internal rules and external standards, notably ISO/IEC 2700x series.
    - Availability: overview available in the Sustainability section of the corporate website.
- Actions and training:
  - Mandatory, structured compliance training for all employees, updated with regulatory/procedural changes; enrollment campaigns, monthly monitoring, reminders; courses require passing a final test.
  - Multidimensional training model to strengthen risk culture, integrated with Model 231/01, assigning relevance levels to material topics.
  - ISMS established with cooperation across all corporate structures and Group companies to protect Group and customer information assets; additional cybersecurity actions referenced under “Privacy” in the Consumers and End Users chapter.
text:
Cybersecurity
IT security is one of the fundamental pillars of the Group’s culture, which is committed to ensuring the resilience,  
robustness and responsiveness of its digital system. 
In this regard, the Group adopts the Group Directive on Logical Security Governance, with the aim of minimising the risks  
associated with cybersecurity  breaches and ensuring adequate protection of data and information throughout their  
life cycle. To this end, the Directive defines the “Information Security Management System” (ISMS) aimed at ensuring  
its safeguarding and protection in all company activities.

text:
Actions
In order to guarantee and ensure that all employees are aware of and understand the values and principles underpinning 
the Group’s activities, a structured training model is in place which sets out that all employees complete their assigned 
courses. 
The courses are updated on the instructions of the compliance function every time there is a regulatory or procedural inno -
vation. As a result, course enrolment campaigns are planned, with monthly monitoring and a reminder plan for all persons 
who do not complete the assigned training. Each online course includes a final test, which must be passed to complete 
the course.
The Group uses a multidimensional training model aimed at a more effective and broad dissemination of risk culture.  
The interaction of the training model with Model 231/01 made it possible to identify the topics material to the latter,  
assigning each of them a level of relevance.
As far as information security is concerned, the Bank, with the support and cooperation of all corporate structures  
and Group companies, has established the Information Security Management System (ISMS), a set of organisational 
structures, processes, procedures and technological solutions adopted for the purpose of protecting the Group’s own  
information assets and the information that customers exchange with the Group. For more information on the actions 
taken by the Group in the area of cybersecurity, please refer to the actions mentioned under “Privacy” in the chapter  
Consumers and End Users.2024 ANNUAL REPORT - Sustainability Reporting 247The following tables also show the percentages of training coverage on 231 relevant and anti-corruption issues for the year

title: Objectives
heading: 4.1.3.4 Objectives
start_phrase: The internal control system, which is a fundamental element of the overall and ordinary governance system of the Group, ensures compliance with the Code of Ethics.
summary:
- Focus on 2024 training coverage across the Group on “231-relevant” compliance topics and anti-corruption, showing near-universal participation (generally 99–100%).
- Headline figures: 16,433 Group employees trained on 231-relevant topics (99%); 16,159 trained on anti-corruption (99%).
- Detailed breakdowns by role and geography:
  - Executives, CEOs and direct reports, middle managers, and employees, with regional splits (Northeast, Northwest, South Central, Islands) all at 99–100% coverage.
  - Function-specific participation and coverage for key C-level areas (Audit, Compliance, Finance, HR, Lending, Operations, Risk, Safety & Security, Legal) and Commercial divisions (Enterprises & Private, Retail, Large Corporate & Investment Banking), with most at 99–100% and a noted 97% for HR.
- Governance objectives: the internal control system underpins Code of Ethics compliance; each function manages and monitors risks, including non-compliance risks.
- Control Functions and Internal Audit: verify regular operations, track risk evolution, and assess the adequacy, functionality, and reliability of the organizational and internal control system.
- Information security: defined roles and responsibilities to ensure separation of duties; an ISMS with security frameworks and indicators for guidance, control, and monitoring; active coordination with authorities and industry associations for alignment and information sharing.
- Whistleblower protection: a formal internal reporting system and Group Directive enable employees and qualified external parties to report fraud, business irregularities, and violations of banking rules and EU law; employees are expected to uphold high ethical standards and report concerns.
- Policy specifics:
  - Scope: all personnel of the Parent Company and Group companies (including Banca Widiba and Monte Paschi Fiduciaria).
  - Oversight: Board of Directors approves the internal reporting system; Board of Statutory Auditors supervises it.
  - Compliance references: Directive 2013/36/EU, Italian Legislative Decree 72/2015, Bank of Italy Circular 285 (11th and 34th updates), and Directive 2019/1937/EU.
  - Availability: policy accessible in the Sustainability section of the Group’s corporate website.
text:
Objectives
The internal control system, which is a fundamental element of the overall and ordinary governance system of the Group, 
ensures compliance with the Code of Ethics. In particular, each corporate function carries out controls aimed at managing, 
monitoring and governing the set of risks relating to the operational areas and responsibilities falling within its competen -
ce, including the risk of non-compliance with the Code.
In addition, there are the Control Functions, which by legislative, regulatory, statutory or self-regulatory provision have 
control tasks, and the Internal Audit Function, which, through audit and control activities, verifies the regular course of 
operations and the development of risks, as well as assessing the completeness, adequacy, functionality and reliability of 
the organisational structure and other components of the internal control system.
With regard to information security, to ensure adequate management thereof, roles and responsibilities relating to informa-
tion security have been defined within the Group so as to separate tasks and areas of responsibility with potential overlaps. BANCA MONTE DEI PASCHI DI SIENA248Furthermore, within the ISMS, security frameworks and indicators are defined for the guidance, control and monitoring of 
protection and safeguard measures of the Group’s general principles, and contacts are maintained with the relevant autho-
rities and industry associations to ensure constant alignment and info-sharing.

summary:
- Describes the Group’s Information Security Management System (ISMS), which sets security frameworks and indicators to guide, control and monitor protection measures, and maintains ongoing coordination with authorities and industry associations for alignment and information sharing.
- Details the whistleblower protection framework, governed by the Group Directive on Internal Violation Reporting Systems, emphasizing ethical conduct, stakeholder considerations, and clear procedures for reporting violations of laws, regulations, internal rules, and EU law.
- Outlines the Group Policy on the management of whistleblowing systems: applies to all personnel of the Parent Company and Group companies (including Banca Widiba and Monte Paschi Fiduciaria); implementation notifications to designated corporate functions; strategic oversight by the Board of Directors and system-wide supervision by the Board of Statutory Auditors; compliance with Directive 2013/36/EU, Legislative Decree 72/2015, Bank of Italy Circular 285 (11th and 34th updates), and Directive 2019/1937/EU; policy available on the corporate website.
- Specifies reporting channels and eligibility: a dedicated internet-accessible IT platform and a telephone line; reporters can include employees, suppliers, consultants, former employees, candidates, shareholders, and persons with administrative, management, or control roles.
- Explains case handling: the Fraud Audit unit within Internal Audit receives and investigates reports; acknowledges receipt within 7 days and provides feedback within 3 months; produces Special Investigation Reports and, where responsibilities are found, follows publication requirements.
- Affirms protections: confidentiality of whistleblowers and reported individuals, protection against retaliation or discrimination for good-faith reports, and penalties for breaches of confidentiality, retaliatory acts, or obstruction.
- Clarifies governance and objectives: the Board of Statutory Auditors oversees the entire system; a Head of Internal Reporting Systems (within Internal Audit) ensures process integrity and reports annually to the Board of Auditors, Board of Directors, Risk and Sustainability Committee, and the Director responsible for internal control and risk management; no quantitative targets set.
- Introduces the anti-corruption framework addressing active and passive corruption and the fight against money laundering and terrorist financing: internal procedures and conduct guidelines for all staff; a rule document providing prevention guidelines that complement the Code of Ethics, Model 231, and procedures for signatory powers, expenditure cycle, and supplier relations.
- Notes the scope of reportable matters includes administrative, accounting, tax, AML/CFT, market abuse, investment services irregularities, and data privacy violations.
text:
Policies
With regard to reports of violations received through the Whistleblowing channel, the Group has set up an internal system, defi-
ning a procedure for the management of reports that employees and qualified external parties may make in relation to events 
of fraud, as well as irregularities in the conduct of business or violations of the rules governing banking activity and of European 
Union law. The relevant process is governed by the Group Directive on the Management of Internal Violation Reporting Systems.
Every employee is expected to actively cooperate in achieving high ethics standards, both directly - by performing their 
duties correctly - and indirectly - by reporting any violations of laws, regulations and procedures that could have a negative 
impact on the Group, its customers, employees and the community in general.
In defining the contents of the Directive, the Group gives due consideration to the interests of key stakeholders, as detailed 
in the Stakeholder Engagement process section of this document.

heading: 4.1.4.2 Actions
start_phrase: Through the dedicated IT platform, which can also be accessed via the internet by “qualified external persons”, or orally via a dedicated telephone service, staff and qualified external persons can report negligent, unlawful, irregular or improper cir- cumstances and conduct relating to their work - which they suspect or have become aware of in the course of their duties.
summary: The excerpt outlines the Group’s whistleblowing framework and anti-corruption governance. It describes a dedicated IT and phone reporting system accessible to employees and qualified external parties (including suppliers, consultants, former and prospective staff, shareholders, and individuals with administrative, management, or control roles) to report suspected negligent, unlawful, irregular, or improper conduct. Reportable matters include administrative and accounting/tax irregularities, AML/CTF violations, market abuse, investment service irregularities, and data privacy breaches. The Fraud Audit unit within Internal Audit receives and investigates reports, acknowledges receipt within seven days, provides follow-up within three months, and issues Special Investigation Reports, including publication when required. The Group guarantees confidentiality and protects whistleblowers from retaliation or discrimination, with penalties for breaches or obstruction. Oversight is provided by the Board of Statutory Auditors, while the Head of Internal Reporting Systems ensures process integrity and reports annually to key governance bodies; no quantitative targets are set. The section also covers active and passive corruption, including AML/CTF, and details policies promoting transparency, accountability, and integrity through anti-corruption procedures and a guideline document that complements the Code of Ethics, Model 231, and procedures governing signatory powers, the expenditure cycle, and supplier relationships.
text:
Actions
Through the dedicated IT platform, which can also be accessed via the internet by “qualified external persons”, or orally via 
a dedicated telephone service, staff and qualified external persons can report negligent, unlawful, irregular or improper cir-
cumstances and conduct relating to their work - which they suspect or have become aware of in the course of their duties. 
The following categories of parties may report information53:  
• personnel, i.e. employees and those who otherwise work on the basis of relationships that determine their inclusion in 
the company organisation;
• qualified external parties, such as: 
 -suppliers, self-employed workers, freelancers and consultants working for the Bank;
 -terminated staff, where the information reported was acquired in the course of the employment relationship;
 -persons for whom the employment relationship has not yet started, where the information reported has been acqui -
red during the selection process;
 -shareholders and persons with administrative, management and control functions. 
The Fraud Audit unit, set up within the Internal Audit function, receives reports and has the task of carrying out  
preliminary checks, investigations and internal assessments, in order to define the legitimacy and reliability of what has been 
reported, obtain evidence and reconstruct the facts. This unit informs the whistleblower, within 7 days from the date of re-
ceipt, that his/her report has been correctly received and taken into account. It also provides feedback to the whistleblower,  
within three months of receipt of the report, on the follow-up action taken.
At the end of each investigation concerning the reports received, a Special Investigation Report is prepared, summarising 
the results of the activities carried out, or, if the investigations reveal responsibilities of employees, a Special Investigation 
Report is prepared and published as required by the Standards in force.
The Group protects whistleblowers who have submitted a report in good faith against retaliatory, discriminatory or in any 
event unfair conduct as a result of the report, which will not, therefore, have a prejudicial effect on continuation of the 
employment relationship. The Group ensures confidentiality of the report and of the personal data of the whistleblower 
and any reported person. Penalties are provided for anyone who violates the measures to protect the confidentiality of the 
whistleblower, commits retaliatory or discriminatory acts against the whistleblower, or takes action to obstruct the report 
or attempt to obstruct it.

Eligible reporters include employees, suppliers, self-employed workers, consultants, former employees (for information acquired during employment), job candidates (for information acquired during selection), shareholders, and those with administrative, management, or control roles. Key documents include the Group Anti-Corruption Policy and the Group Policy on Combating Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing, both approved by the Board of Directors and available on the corporate website. Policies apply to all Group personnel and entities acting on the Group’s behalf, with control activities assigned to Corporate Control Functions. text:
Policies 
The Group promotes the principles of transparency, accountability and integrity in its relations with public administrations 
and external staff by adopting internal anti-corruption procedures and courses of action for all personnel.
To reinforce this commitment, the Group has issued a rule document containing guidelines for the prevention of corruptive 
events, which constitutes the framework for the prevention of corruption risks. The document complements and reinfor-
ces the anti-corruption policy already adopted by the Group over time through the new Code of Ethics, Model 231 and the 
provision of specific procedures for managing the exercise of signatory powers, the expenditure cycle and relations with 
suppliers. 
53 Whistleblowing reports include, but are not limited to, administrative irregularities and accounting and tax compliance, potential or actual violations of the 
provisions laid down to prevent money laundering and the financing of terrorism, market abuse (insider trading, manipulation) and other irregularities in 
investment services and activities, and violations of data privacy regulations.BANCA MONTE DEI PASCHI DI SIENA250The Group also pays the utmost attention to compliance with national and international regulations aimed at combating 
money laundering and terrorist financing54. For this reason, it has adopted a “Policy on Combating Money Laundering and 
Terrorist Financing”, reflecting its commitment to fight the aforementioned criminal phenomena on an international basis, 
devoting particular attention to the tools to use in this fight, in the knowledge that the pursuit of profitability and efficiency 
must be combined with the continuous and effective monitoring of the integrity of corporate structures.
In defining the contents of the cited documents, the Group gives due consideration to the interests of key stakeholders, as 
detailed in the Stakeholder Engagement process section of this document.

title: Actions
heading: 4.1.5.2 Actions
start_phrase: The Group operates in line with its values and with a sense of responsibility towards society by applying “zero tolerance” towards any corrupt practice (direct or indirect, public or private, external or within the organisation, instigated, attemp- ted, committed), to ensure that its staff and all persons working for it comply with anti-corruption regulations, adopting all measures necessary to prevent and effectively counter the risk.
summary:
- Focus: Governance, policies, actions, controls, training, and oversight related to anti-corruption and the prevention of money laundering and terrorist financing (AML/CTF) within Banca Monte dei Paschi di Siena Group, as part of its Sustainability Reporting.
- Policy framework:
  - Group Anti-Corruption Policy: Sets principles and conduct rules for all employees and third parties acting for the Group; approved by the Board; control activities assigned to Corporate Control Functions; aligned with UN Global Compact, UNEP Principles for Responsible Banking, and guidance from OECD, UN, G20, Transparency International, and the Wolfsberg Group; available on the corporate website.
  - Group AML/CTF Policy: Defines the Group’s global AML/CTF approach for the Parent Company and all subsidiaries; Board approves the policy and annual AML report (including ML/TF risk self-assessment and activity plan); aligned with national, EU, and international standards; available on the corporate website.
- Stakeholders: Policy design considers interests identified through the Group’s Stakeholder Engagement process.
- Zero tolerance and disciplinary regime: The Group applies zero tolerance to all forms of corruption (public/private, internal/external, direct/indirect) and foresees disciplinary actions up to termination for violations.
- Risk assessment and scope:
  - Periodic self-assessments of corruption risks across all business processes; biennial identification of high-risk areas (e.g., suppliers, JVs/M&A, gifts/entertainment, events/sponsorships, hiring, credit disbursement, procurement, consultancy, subsidised finance, political contributions/donations/memberships/non-profit, management of public services).
  - Latest 2024 assessment found potential risks across structures but no need for additional measures beyond existing safeguards.
  - Explicit prohibition of political contributions and heightened controls in dealings with Public Administration.
- Anti-corruption program and training:
  - Ongoing risk self-assessments by functions and employee awareness/training.
  - Training content updated by the Training function with Compliance validation upon regulatory/procedural changes or audit findings.
  - Specialized training for Internal Audit’s Fraud Audit staff (including international certification paths such as CFE).
  - Board induction for subsidiaries on administrative liability and Group 231 Models.
- AML/CTF controls:
  - Identification of applicable regulations, impact assessment, and updates to internal rules.
  - IT systems for risk management, due diligence, data retention, continuous customer/transaction monitoring, detection of potentially suspicious activity, and reporting to the Financial Information unit.
  - Ongoing assessment of risk management processes and internal control adequacy.
  - Mandatory AML/CTF training for all employees.
- Roles and responsibilities:
  - Compliance Function: Identifies corruption-risk processes and evaluates safeguards; coordinates rule application and training; provides advisory support; partners with HR on info-training programs.
  - 2024 Compliance Plan: Approved 6 Feb 2024; 797 audits executed vs 692 planned; 758 conformity opinions and 649 validation opinions issued.
  - Internal Audit: Performs third-level controls within the Internal Control System.
  - AML Function (Parent Company) and Chief Risk Officer’s department (Group level): Monitor AML/CTF risks; CRO reports directly to the Board and centralizes duties for Italian subsidiaries.
- Targets: The Group ensures prevention of active and passive corruption (including AML/CTF) but has not set quantitative targets.
text:
Actions
The Group operates in line with its values and with a sense of responsibility towards society by applying “zero tolerance” 
towards any corrupt practice (direct or indirect, public or private, external or within the organisation, instigated, attemp-
ted, committed), to ensure that its staff and all persons working for it comply with anti-corruption regulations, adopting 
all measures necessary to prevent and effectively counter the risk. In this regard, the Group is committed to carrying out 
a self-assessment of risks, to be submitted periodically to the corporate functions in order to assess their likelihood of 
occurrence and the effectiveness of the relevant regulatory and control measures. 
The Group periodically identifies, at intervals of no less than two years, the main areas considered to be at risk of corruption 
related to significantly sensitive activities55 and, for these, it supplements the existing processes with precise indications 
aimed at preventing any episodes. In addition to regulatory sanctions, any violation of anti-corruption provisions may lead 
to disciplinary action against the employee responsible, up to the most serious sanction of termination of employment.
54 These concepts refer to the risk arising from the breach of legal, regulatory and self-governance provisions necessary for preventing use of the financial 
system for purposes of money laundering, terrorist financing or the financing of programmes for the development of weapons of mass destruction, as well 
as the risk of involvement in money laundering, terrorist financing or the financing of programmes for the development of weapons of mass destruction.
55 These include: appointments of suppliers; joint ventures, acquisitions and disposals of company shareholdings; gifts and entertainment; events and 
sponsorships; job offers; disbursement of credit; management of the liability cycle (expenditure); consultancy; transactions in which the Bank is a public 
service provider (subsidised finance); political contributions, donations, membership fees, non-profit; management of public services.2024 ANNUAL REPORT - Sustainability Reporting 251For each business process, the corruption risks to which the Group is potentially exposed are assessed56. The results of the 
last assessment exercise carried out in 2024 showed that, despite the existence of potential risks on all Group structures, 
there was no need to take further action than the safeguards currently in place.  With specific reference to relations with the 
Public Administration, which are particularly sensitive to the risk of corruption, the Group expressly prohibits the granting 
of political contributions or any disbursement in cash or in kind t o support a particular political cause. 
In relation to the safeguards put in place with regard to active and passive corruption, the Group is committed to complying 
with an anti-corruption programme that provides for:
• a risk self assessment activity to be submitted periodically to the corporate functions with reference to the risks/safe-
guards inherent in their respective processes;
• training and awareness-raising plans for employees.
The Training function updates the contents of the anti-corruption course on the instructions of the Compliance function 
(responsible for the validation of the contents) whenever there are regulatory or procedural changes or gaps in the audit.
In addition, the training plan for the Internal Audit function includes specific training activities for Fraud Audit staff, inclu -
ding a training pill and a more structured course, including through the use of international certification paths (e.g. Certified 
Fraud Examiner).
For the Boards of Directors of the subsidiaries, specific board induction sessions on administrative liability of entities and 
the structure of the Group’s 231 Models. In the area of combating money laundering and terrorist financing, the Group’s 
controls consist of the activities listed below: 
• identifying applicable regulations, assessing the impact on processes and procedures, updating the internal regulatory 
framework; 
• implementing suitable IT procedures for consistent risk management, due diligence, data and information storage, 
continuous monitoring of customers and transactions, detection of potentially suspicious transactions and reporting to 
the Financial Information unit; 
• assessing the adequacy of the risk management process and the suitability of the internal control system and proce -
dures;
• providing anti-money laundering and anti-terrorism training to all employees.

summary:
- Scope: Anti-corruption, anti–money laundering (AML) and counter-terrorist financing (CTF) governance, controls, training, and metrics within the Group’s 2024 Sustainability Reporting.
- Risk assessment and policy: Corruption risks are assessed across all business processes; 2024 results found potential risks everywhere but deemed current safeguards adequate. Strict prohibition on political contributions or any support to political causes, with heightened focus on interactions with Public Administration.
- Anti-corruption program: Periodic risk self-assessments by functions; employee training and awareness plans. Training content is updated by the Training function under Compliance validation when regulations/procedures change or audits reveal gaps.

The Parent Company’s AML function monitors AML/CTF risks; at Group level, the Chief Risk Officer (reporting to the Board) centrally oversees these duties for Italian subsidiaries. Corporate bodies are involved with defined roles per the Internal Control System. No quantitative prevention targets are set.

- Training metrics (2024): 100% of Parent Company staff are enrolled due to universal exposure to corruption risk. Training recipients included 16,321 workers in functions at risk (out of 16,439 total), 155 executive managers, and 7 members of administrative/management/supervisory bodies. Delivery included classroom (e.g., 19.0 hours for functions at risk; 5.0 for administrative bodies) and computer-based training (e.g., 12,227.0 hours for functions at risk; 116.3 for executives; 2.0 for administrative bodies). offences to be provided to Group employees.

Where use of proceeds is known, no eligible/aligned exposures were identified under the screening criteria.

Loans for building renovations and motor vehicles excluded due to insufficient data to identify “green loans.” Alignment applies technical criteria differentiating buildings constructed before/after 31 Dec 2020. NFRD perimeter broadened to include entities whose parents are subject to NFRD.

Alignment applies screening criteria distinguishing buildings constructed before/after 31 Dec 2020; for pre‑2020 assets not EPC class A, alignment may be met if in the top 15% of national/regional building stock for primary energy needs, supported by private studies (newly available in 2024).

text:
Introduction
The tables below show the disclosure requirements under Article 8 of the Disclosures Delegated Act supplementing  
the EU Taxonomy Regulation (2020/852)57.
These obligations require financial firms to report KPIs for eligibility and alignment with the Taxonomy commencing the 
calendar year 2023. This disclosure aims to provide transparency about sustainability and facilitate the transition to a 
low-carbon economy. In particular, Article 8 of the Regulation requires companies within the scope of the Non-Financial 
Reporting Directive (NFRD) 2014/95/EU to publish information on how and to what extent their economic activities qualify 
as “environmentally sustainable” according to the Taxonomy Regulation. The result is presented as the Green Asset Ratio 
(GAR), i.e. exposure to taxonomy-aligned assets (numerator) divided by total assets (denominator).
At 31 December 2024, the turnover-based GAR and the capex-based GAR were 1.06% (0.50% at 31 December 2023)  
and 1.15% (0.53% at 31 December 2023), respectively, while total GAR assets were EUR 94,586 mln (EUR 94,254 mln  
at 31 December 2023).
To calculate GAR at the present date, we would need to have the actual data disclosed by counterparties in order to mea-
sure the banks’ taxonomy-related KPIs. What this means is that companies that are not required to publish non-financial 
disclosures (NFRD) are excluded from the calculation, and this lack of data is reflected in the GAR for the bank.

title: Methodology
heading: 5.1.2 Methodology
start_phrase: The main methodological choices adopted by the Group on the basis of current regulations are outlined below.
summary:
- Context and purpose: Part of the Sustainability Reporting section detailing Article 8 EU Taxonomy (Reg. 2020/852) disclosures for credit institutions. From 2023, financial firms must report eligibility and alignment KPIs to enhance transparency and support the low‑carbon transition. Scope follows the NFRD (2014/95/EU).

- Key metrics reported (as of 31 Dec 2024):
  - Turnover-based Green Asset Ratio (GAR): 1.06% (0.50% at 31 Dec 2023).
  - Capex-based GAR: 1.15% (0.53% at 31 Dec 2023).
  - Total GAR assets (denominator): EUR 94,586 million (EUR 94,254 million at 31 Dec 2023).
  - Note: GAR depends on counterparties’ disclosed data; exposures to entities outside NFRD scope are excluded, which impacts the ratio.

- Methodological framework:
  - KPIs per Annex V of Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/2178.
  - GAR defined as exposures to taxonomy‑aligned assets divided by total covered assets (gross carrying amount of total assets excluding trading book exposures and exposures to central governments, central banks, and supranational issuers).

- Key methodological decisions:
  - Financial undertakings and entities not obliged to publish non-financial information:
    - Where use of proceeds is unknown (assessed with an external provider), exposures are weighted by counterparties’ reported Taxonomy turnover and CapEx KPIs across the six environmental objectives.
    - Where use of proceeds is known, no taxonomy-eligible and aligned exposures were identified under Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/2139.
    - Following European Commission FAQs (21 Dec 2023 and Nov 2024), NFRD counterparties now also include entities whose parent companies are subject to NFRD, expanding scope versus 2023.
  - Guaranteed household loans:
    - Eligibility limited to loans secured by residential real estate.
    - Building renovations and motor vehicle purchases excluded due to insufficient data to tag “green loans.”
    - Alignment screening applies criteria for buildings constructed before/after 31 Dec 2020. For pre‑2020 buildings lacking EPC class A, the Group used the “top 15%” primary energy performance criterion based on private studies (new in 2024).
  - Flows: Defined as gross new exposures; only positive flows are counted (no netting of repayments or sales).
  - Assets under management (AuM): KPI calculated as the share of equity and debt issued by NFRD‑subject companies within total AuM equity and debt.

- Comparability note: Templates as of 31 Dec 2023 are disclosed, but year‑on‑year comparisons are not fully homogeneous due to 2024 scope changes (notably inclusion of entities with NFRD‑subject parent companies).

- Gas and Nuclear templates: In line with Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/1214 (amending 2021/2139), the Group reports eligibility, alignment, and non‑eligibility for gas and nuclear activities. These templates cover only non‑financial companies that disclosed the relevant KPIs in their 2023 reporting.
text:
Methodology
The main methodological choices adopted by the Group on the basis of current regulations are outlined below.  
In particular, the Group has adopted the key performance indicators (KPIs) set out in Annex V of Commission Delegated 
Regulation (EU) 2021/2178. 
The Green Asset Ratio (GAR) is the ratio of (i) exposures to taxonomy-aligned assets to (ii) the value of total covered assets58: 
The following methodological decisions were made to determine the share of taxonomy-eligible and taxonomy-aligned 
exposures:
• Financial	 undertakings	 and	undertakings	 not	obliged	 to	publish	 non-financial	 information	 (Legislative	 Decree	
254/2016 and/or Regulation (EU) 2013/34/EU- NFRD):  exposures where the use of proceeds is not known  - as deter-
mined with the support of an external provider - were weighted by the turnover and CapEx KPIs, in relation to taxonomy 
eligible and aligned activities for the six environmental objectives, published by these counterparties in their respective 
non-financial statements. On the other hand, taking into account the technical screening criteria set out in Delegated 
Regulation 2021/2139 EU, there are no taxonomy eligible and aligned exposures where the use of proceeds is known. In 
light of the interpretative clarifications provided by the European Commission in the FAQs on 21 December 2023 and in 
November 2024, the identified NFRD counterparties also included - in contrast with the situation at 31 December 2023 
- counterparties whose parent companies are subject to non-financial reporting requirements;
• guaranteed household loans:  Based on Delegated Regulation 2021/2139, only loans secured by residential real estate 
were considered for eligibility. On the other hand, loans for “building renovations” under the same regulation and for the 
purchase of “motor vehicles” were out of scope due to the lack of specific information on identifying “green loans”. To 
determine alignment KPIs, the technical screening criteria set forth in the aforementioned Delegated Regulation were 
applied to distinguish between real estate constructed before and after 31 December 2020. For 2024, with regards to 
buildings constructed before 2020 that do not meet the requirement of a class-A energy performance certificate, the 
Group applied the criterion – in light of the abovementioned clarifications provided by the European Commission – of 
whether the building was included in the top 15% of the national or regional building stock in terms of primary energy 
requirements. This was because it was able to make use of studies published by private entities, unlike in the previous 
financial year;
57 For a full discussion of the relevant regulatory framework, please refer to the section entitled “Disclosure pursuant to Article 8 of Regulation (EU) 2020/852 
(Taxonomy Regulation)” in Section 2 “Environmental Information” of this Sustainability Report.
58 In keeping with EU Delegated Regulation 2021/2178, “total GAR” means the gross carrying amount of the Group’s total assets less trading book exposures 
and exposures to central governments, central banks and supranational issuers.BANCA MONTE DEI PASCHI DI SIENA254• Flows: In line with Regulation (EU) 2021/2178, the Group considers the amount of new exposures based on the gross 
book value as the flow; only positive flows are considered without deducting the amounts of loan repayments or sales 
of debt/equity instruments that occurred in the same period;
• assets under management: the ratio of the portfolio of equity and debt securities held as Assets Under Management 
and issued by financial and non-financial companies subject to mandatory NFRD to total equity and debt securities held 
in as Assets Under Management was considered. 
Finally, as required by the Regulation, templates referring to 31 December 2023 have been published. However, it should 
be noted that comparisons are not homogeneous as a result of the above-mentioned changes to the scope of the 2024 
disclosure.

start_phrase: In line with Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/1214 of 9 March 2022 amending Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/2139, the Group publishes templates for the alignment, eligibility and non-eligibility of gas and nuclear activities.
summary:
- Regulatory basis and methodology: Disclosures prepared under EU Taxonomy Regulation (EU) 2021/2178, with “flows” defined as new exposures at gross book value (only positive flows), and an Assets Under Management ratio limited to securities issued by companies subject to mandatory NFRD. Templates are referenced to 31 Dec 2023; 2024 scope changes make year-on-year comparisons non-homogeneous.
- Gas & Nuclear disclosures: In line with Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/1214, publication of templates on eligibility, alignment, and non-eligibility of gas and nuclear activities, limited to non-financial companies that reported the relevant KPIs in 2023.
- Key KPIs for credit institutions (Annex VI):
  - Main KPI Green Asset Ratio (GAR) – stock:
    - 2024: Environmentally sustainable assets €997m (Turnover) and €1,089m (Capex); % KPI 1.05% (Turnover) and 1.15% (Capex); coverage over total assets 75.77%; assets excluded from numerator 44.96% and from denominator 24.23%.
    - 2023: €467m (Turnover) and €496m (Capex); % KPI 0.50% and 0.53%; coverage 75.52%; excluded from numerator 49.52% and from denominator 24.48%.
  - Additional KPI GAR – flows:
    - 2024: €587m (Turnover) and €1,055m (Capex); % KPI 0.62% and 1.12%; coverage over total assets 6.54%.
    - 2023: €141m (Turnover) and €151m (Capex); % KPI 0.15% and 0.16%.
  - Trading book and fee/commission income: not applicable/blank. Financial guarantees and AUM show small aligned portions (e.g., 2024 FG 1.06% Turnover, 2.75% Capex; AUM 3.45% Turnover, 7.24% Capex).
- Detailed GAR stock breakdowns (2024 and 2023) by:
  - Counterparty type (financial undertakings, non-financial undertakings, households), product (loans and advances, debt securities, equity), and environmental objectives (CCM, CCA, WTR, CE, PPC, BIO).
  - Classification of aligned activities into use-of-proceeds, transitional, and enabling.
  - Households, especially residential mortgage loans, represent the bulk of taxonomy-eligible exposure (2024: €30.354bn eligible; €867m aligned).
  - Non-financial undertakings contribute to aligned amounts; financial undertakings show limited alignment; insurance negligible.
- Scope of assets in GAR:
  - Numerator exclusions captured (but included in denominator): SMEs/NFCs not subject to NFRD, non-EU counterparties not subject to NFRD, derivatives, on-demand interbank, cash and cash-like, and other assets.
  - Total GAR assets and assets not covered for GAR provided; the latter include central governments, central banks, and trading book exposures.
- Off-balance sheet exposures (to undertakings subject to NFRD): Reported aligned amounts for financial guarantees and AUM, with debt/equity splits.

title: Assets for the GAR (stock) - Capex calculation
heading: 1.Assets for the GAR (stock) - Capex calculation
start_phrase: In milion of Eur 2024
summary:
- Extract from Banca Monte dei Paschi di Siena’s 2024 Annual Report (Sustainability Reporting) detailing EU Taxonomy and Green Asset Ratio (GAR) disclosures.
- Presents the “Assets for the GAR (stock)” with a CapEx-based view and a comparative 2024 vs 2023 snapshot, in millions of euros.
- Breaks down GAR-covered assets (included in numerator and denominator) by counterparty and instrument: financial undertakings (credit institutions, other financial corporations, management companies, insurance), non‑financial undertakings, and households (notably mortgages collateralised by residential property). Also shows collateral obtained.
- For each exposure, reports taxonomy eligibility and alignment across the six environmental objectives: Climate Change Mitigation (CCM), Climate Change Adaptation (CCA), Water and Marine Resources (WTR), Circular Economy (CE), Pollution Prevention and Control (PPC), and Biodiversity and Ecosystems (BIO).
- Further classifies aligned exposures by “use of proceeds,” “transitional,” and “enabling” categories.
- Details assets excluded from the GAR numerator (but included in the denominator), including SMEs and NFCs not subject to NFRD disclosure, non‑EU counterparties not subject to NFRD, derivatives, on‑demand interbank loans, cash and cash‑related assets, and other assets (e.g., goodwill).
- Summarizes total GAR assets, assets not covered for GAR (central governments, central banks, trading book), and total assets for both 2024 and 2023.
- Includes off‑balance sheet exposures for undertakings subject to NFRD (financial guarantees and assets under management), with “of which” breakdowns for debt and equity and their taxonomy eligibility/alignment.
- Provides a sectoral (NACE 4‑digit) view of stock aligned exposures on a turnover basis, listing sectors such as electricity production/transmission/distribution, shipbuilding, machinery and equipment manufacturing, petroleum products, chemicals/synthetic fibres, electronics and instruments—showing gross carrying amounts and the portion environmentally sustainable under each objective.

heading: 2. GAR sector information of the stock aligned exposures - Turnover
start_phrase: 1 Credit institutions must report in this template information on exposures in the banking book with the sectors covered by the taxonomy (NACE sectors 4 levels of detail), using the relevant NACE codes on the basis of the counterparty’s principal activity.
summary:
- Extract from Banca Monte dei Paschi di Siena’s 2024 Annual Report – Sustainability Reporting, focused on Green Asset Ratio (GAR) disclosure.
- Presents GAR sector information for the stock of taxonomy‑aligned exposures using two KPIs:
  - Turnover-based alignment.
  - Capex-based alignment (partial table shown).
- Granular breakdown by sector at NACE Rev. 2, 4‑digit code level, with line‑by‑line figures across numerous industries (manufacturing, energy and utilities, waste and remediation, construction and civil engineering, transport and logistics, telecoms and data services, real estate, business services, and other services).
- Discloses, in EUR million, for each sector and counterparty category:
  - Gross carrying amount.
  - “Of which environmentally sustainable” amounts under EU Taxonomy objectives: Climate Change Mitigation (CCM), Climate Change Adaptation (CCA), Water and Marine Resources (WTR), Circular Economy (CE), Pollution Prevention and Control (PPC), and Biodiversity and Ecosystems (BIO), plus a total across all objectives.
- Counterparty segmentation distinguishes:
  - Non-financial corporates subject to NFRD.
  - SMEs and other non-financial corporates not subject to NFRD.
- Illustrative sector entries include electricity production/transmission/distribution, water collection/treatment/supply, waste treatment, shipbuilding, machinery and equipment, petroleum products, construction of roads, telecoms and data processing, and others, showing both gross exposures and the subset deemed environmentally sustainable; many sectors display low or zero alignment, with some notable aligned amounts in utilities, water services, waste management, shipbuilding, and telecoms.
- Provides a 2023 comparative table for turnover-based alignment to enable year‑on‑year sectoral comparison.
- Methodological notes specify:
  - NACE assignment is based on the immediate counterparty’s principal activity.
  - Joint exposures are classified by the borrower most relevant/decisive for granting the exposure.
  - Reporting must follow the required 4‑digit NACE disaggregation.
- Bilingual column headers (English/Italian) indicate “of which environmentally sustainable” values; figures are presented in EUR million.

title: GAR sector information of the stock aligned exposures - Capex
heading: 2. GAR sector information of the stock aligned exposures - Capex
start_phrase: Breakdown by sector - NACE 4 digits level (code and label) Climate Change Mitigation
summary:
- Focus: Banca Monte dei Paschi di Siena’s EU Taxonomy Green Asset Ratio (GAR) disclosures, with a sectoral view of taxonomy-aligned exposures based on Capex, and the GAR “stock” turnover calculation for 2024, plus a compact 2023 sectoral comparison.

- Scope and structure:
  - Detailed breakdown by NACE 4‑digit sector of gross carrying amounts (EUR million) and “of which environmentally sustainable” amounts for each of the six environmental objectives: Climate Change Mitigation (CCM), Climate Change Adaptation (CCA), Water and Marine Resources (WTR), Circular Economy (CE), Pollution Prevention and Control (PPC), Biodiversity and Ecosystems (BIO).
  - Split by counterparty type: non‑financial corporates subject to NFRD vs SMEs/other NFCs not subject to NFRD.
  - Coverage spans energy, manufacturing, utilities, construction, transport/logistics, telecoms, real estate, and business services.

- 2024 sector highlights (examples from the extract):
  - Electricity networks and generation show notable aligned portions (e.g., transmission and distribution with high CCM alignment; electricity production with aligned amounts reported).
  - Water and waste utilities contribute aligned exposures (water collection/treatment/supply and treatment/disposal of non‑hazardous waste show aligned amounts across CCM, WTR, CE, and PPC).
  - Civil engineering and roads display some CCM‑aligned shares.
  - Transport‑related services (service activities incidental to land transport) include meaningful aligned exposures.
  - Selected manufacturing (e.g., measuring instruments, engines/turbines, cables) and telecoms (wired telecommunications) show exposures with modest aligned components.
  - Several sectors carry exposure but no aligned share (e.g., crude oil extraction, some retail/manufacturing activities).

- 2023 comparison:
  - A condensed table lists selected NACE sectors with gross vs aligned amounts, enabling a year‑over‑year view of taxonomy alignment for key activities (e.g., shipbuilding, machinery, electricity, gas trading, postal/courier).

- GAR “Total assets for the stock – Turnover (%)” (2024):
  - About 32.7% of total assets are GAR‑covered.
  - Taxonomy‑aligned shares are small overall, concentrated in CCM (≈1.06% of total assets), with limited alignment in CCA (~0.01%), WTR (~0.06%), and CE (~0.02%); PPC and BIO are negligible in the extract.
  - By counterparty:
    - Households (primarily residential mortgages) constitute the largest covered share and the bulk of the aligned CCM component (~0.93% via green/energy‑efficient mortgages).
    - Non‑financial undertakings contribute ~0.11% aligned.
    - Financial undertakings contribute ~0.02% aligned.
  - Instrument split includes loans and advances, debt securities (including use‑of‑proceeds), and equity; “use of proceeds,” “transitional,” and “enabling” flags are disclosed but minimal in the excerpt.

- Measurement notes:
  - Figures are gross carrying amounts (EUR million) for sector tables and proportions of total assets for the GAR turnover calculation.
  - Assets held for trading are excluded from the GAR scope.

title: Total assets for the stock GAR - Turnover (%) calculation
heading: 3.Total assets for the stock GAR - Turnover (%) calculation
start_phrase: % (compared to total covered assets in the denominator)2024
summary:
- Focus: EU Taxonomy Green Asset Ratio (GAR) disclosures for Banca Monte dei Paschi di Siena’s stock of assets within the Sustainability Reporting section of the 2024 Annual Report.
- Scope and methodology: GAR calculated on assets covered in both numerator and denominator, excluding held-for-trading instruments; includes breakdowns by environmental objectives (CCM, CCA, WTR, CE, PPC, BIO), taxonomy eligibility vs taxonomy alignment, and flags for Use of Proceeds, enabling, and transitional activities.
- 2024 Turnover-based GAR: Detailed split by counterparty/asset class (financial undertakings, non-financial undertakings, households, collateral) and by instrument (loans and advances, debt securities including Use of Proceeds, equity). Taxonomy-aligned exposure is concentrated in Climate Change Mitigation and remains minimal across other objectives; Use of Proceeds/enabling/transitional shares are negligible.
- 2023 Turnover-based GAR (comparative): Same structure enabling year-on-year comparison. Shows a lower taxonomy-aligned share in CCM versus 2024, indicating improvement in 2024 primarily under Climate Change Mitigation.
- 2024 Capex-based GAR: Parallel breakdown to the turnover metric, generally showing slightly higher taxonomy-aligned proportions than the turnover view, again mainly under Climate Change Mitigation; other objectives remain marginal.
- Portfolio composition insights: Households—especially mortgages collateralised by residential property—constitute the bulk of GAR-covered assets; non-financial corporates contribute a small but positive share of taxonomy-eligible/aligned exposure; financial sector exposures show minimal alignment.
- Other notes: Collateral obtained (repossessed properties) is marginal; building renovation and motor vehicle loan categories are reported but with negligible or zero contributions; local government financing is not present in the covered scope.

heading: 3.Total assets for the stock GAR - Capex (%) calculation

summary:
- Extract from the Sustainability Reporting section of Banca Monte dei Paschi di Siena’s 2024 Annual Report presenting EU Taxonomy key performance indicators (Green Asset Ratio, GAR).
- Provides two KPI views:
  - Stock GAR based on Capex (%): full 2024 disclosure with a like-for-like 2023 comparison.
  - Flow GAR based on Turnover (%): 2024 disclosure.
- Structure and scope:
  - Breakdowns by EU environmental objectives: Climate Change Mitigation (CCM), Climate Change Adaptation (CCA), Water and Marine Resources (WTR), Circular Economy (CE), Pollution Prevention and Control (PPC), Biodiversity and Ecosystems (BIO).
  - For each objective: “taxonomy-eligible” vs “environmentally sustainable (taxonomy-aligned)”, with flags for Use of Proceeds, transitional, and enabling activities.
  - Asset classes and counterparties covered: loans and advances, debt securities (including use-of-proceeds bonds), equity instruments; financial undertakings (credit institutions, other financial corporations, management companies, insurance undertakings), non‑financial undertakings, households (notably loans collateralised by residential property), local government financing, and collateral obtained.
  - Denominator and coverage details: “not HfT eligible for GAR calculation,” total GAR assets, and proportion of total assets covered.
- Main findings for Stock GAR (Capex):
  - Households—especially loans collateralised by residential immovable property—represent the largest share of covered assets.
  - Taxonomy alignment increases year over year: overall aligned share rises from 0.53% (2023) to 1.16% (2024).
  - Non‑financial undertakings show growth in alignment (roughly doubling from 2023 to 2024), with small aligned portions mainly in climate change mitigation and, to a lesser extent, circular economy and water.
  - Financial undertakings contribute marginally to aligned exposure; equity instruments are largely absent.
  - Use-of-proceeds, enabling, and transitional categories appear but remain minimal.
  - No contributions from building renovation or motor vehicle loans; local government financing and collateral obtained are immaterial.
- Main findings for Flow GAR (Turnover) 2024:
  - Presents eligible and aligned shares with the same objective and sectoral breakdown.
  - Overall taxonomy-aligned share is modest (around 0.62%), with most contribution from households and non‑financial undertakings; financial undertakings add a small amount.
  - Use-of-proceeds, enabling, and transitional exposures remain limited.
- Cross-cutting observation:
  - Eligibility is higher than alignment; alignment is concentrated in climate change mitigation, with minor presence in adaptation, circular economy, and water; pollution and biodiversity exposures are negligible.

title: Total assets for the flow GAR - Turnover calculation
heading: 4.Total assets for the flow GAR - Turnover calculation
start_phrase: % (compared to total covered assets in the denominator)2024
summary:
- Section of Banca Monte dei Paschi di Siena’s 2024 Sustainability Report disclosing EU Taxonomy “flow GAR” (Green Asset Ratio) metrics.
- Presents detailed tables for:
  - Flow GAR – Turnover calculation, with 2024 results and 2023 comparatives.
  - Flow GAR – Capex (%) calculation for 2024.
- Scope and structure:
  - Assets covered: loans and advances, debt securities and equity instruments not held for trading (HfT), shown in both numerator and denominator.
  - Breakdowns by counterparty/asset class: financial undertakings (credit institutions, other financial corporations, insurance), non‑financial undertakings, households (notably mortgages), local governments, and collateral obtained.
  - Environmental objectives reported per EU Taxonomy: Climate Change Mitigation (CCM), Climate Change Adaptation (CCA), Water and Marine Resources (WTR), Circular Economy (CE), Pollution Prevention and Control (PPC), and Biodiversity and Ecosystems (BIO).
  - For each objective: taxonomy-eligible vs taxonomy-aligned proportions, plus “Use of Proceeds,” and flags for “transitional” and “enabling” activities.
  - “Proportion of total assets covered” indicates the share of assets included in the GAR denominator.
- Key observations from the disclosed figures:
  - 2024 turnover-based GAR shows higher taxonomy-aligned shares than 2023, especially under Climate Change Mitigation, with broader coverage across non‑financial undertakings and households.
  - Households (primarily residential mortgage loans) constitute a significant share of taxonomy-eligible exposure under CCM; alignment is reported but remains a smaller subset.
  - Non‑financial undertakings show measurable eligible and some aligned exposures spanning CCM and limited contributions across other objectives; financial undertakings’ contributions are small.
  - Use-of-proceeds instruments and “transitional/enabling” classifications are reported but generally limited or zero in most categories.
  - Several categories (e.g., local government financing, collateral obtained) are negligible or not contributing to the GAR.
  - 2024 Capex-based GAR percentages are provided with similar sectoral and objective breakdowns, indicating notable contributions from non‑financial undertakings and households and, overall, higher eligible shares than in turnover.
- The tables conclude with “Total GAR assets” lines summarizing eligible and aligned figures and the proportion of total assets covered for each year (turnover) and for 2024 (capex).

summary:
- Extract from Banca Monte dei Paschi di Siena’s 2024 Annual Report – Sustainability Reporting detailing EU Taxonomy disclosures.
- Section 4 reports “Total assets for the flow GAR – Capex (%)” with:
  - A breakdown by the six environmental objectives (Climate Change Mitigation, Climate Change Adaptation, Water and Marine Resources, Circular Economy, Pollution Prevention and Control, Biodiversity and Ecosystems).
  - Separate disclosure of taxonomy-eligible vs. taxonomy-aligned shares, and tags for Use of Proceeds, transitional, and enabling activities.
  - Granular splits by counterparty/asset class: financial undertakings (including credit institutions and insurance), non-financial corporates, households (notably mortgages secured by residential property), local governments, and collateral obtained.
  - 2024 figures show Climate Change Mitigation as the dominant objective, with additional (smaller) contributions to other objectives; households’ mortgage book and non-financial corporates are key drivers of eligibility/alignment.
  - A 2023 comparative table evidences much lower aligned values and minimal contributions outside Climate Change Mitigation in the prior year, enabling a year-on-year view of progress and methodology coverage (including the proportion of total assets covered in the denominator).
- Section 5 presents Alignment and Eligibility KPIs for off-balance sheet exposures (Financial Guarantees and Assets Under Management), covering:
  - Capex and Turnover KPIs, each shown for Stock and Flow.
  - Objective-level splits, with taxonomy-eligible and taxonomy-aligned shares and identification of enabling and transitional components.
  - 2024 results indicate higher taxonomy alignment within Assets under Management than within Financial Guarantees, with Climate Change Mitigation again the primary contributor; enabling activities are more prevalent than transitional ones.
- Overall, the excerpt provides a quantitative, objective-by-objective and portfolio-slice-by-portfolio-slice view of EU Taxonomy eligibility and alignment for both on-balance sheet (GAR) and off-balance sheet activities (FinGuar and AuM), with year-on-year comparatives and disclosure of the scope/coverage of assets used in the calculations.

summary:
- Presents EU Taxonomy alignment and eligibility KPIs for off-balance sheet exposures of Banca Monte dei Paschi di Siena, covering Financial Guarantees (FinGuar KPI) and Assets Under Management (AuM KPI).
- Discloses percentages relative to total eligible off-balance sheet assets for 2024, with prior-year (2023) comparatives.
- Breaks data into four KPI lenses: Capex Stock, Turnover Stock, Capex Flows, and Turnover Flows.
- Details performance across the six environmental objectives: Climate Change Mitigation (CCM), Climate Change Adaptation (CCA), Water and Marine Resources (WTR), Circular Economy (CE), Pollution Prevention and Control (PPC), and Biodiversity and Ecosystems (BIO).
- For each objective, shows:
  - Share toward taxonomy-relevant sectors (taxonomy-eligible).
  - Portion that is environmentally sustainable (taxonomy-aligned).
  - Further categorization of aligned exposures by Use of Proceeds, and by enabling and transitional activities.
- Provides totals aggregating all environmental objectives for each KPI and product category.
- Highlights a significant increase in 2024 taxonomy-related and aligned percentages versus very small figures in 2023 across both Financial Guarantees and AuM.
- Includes an “Additional information on nuclear energy and fossil gas activities” template:
  - Nuclear energy: no activities/exposures in loans and advances, guarantees, or AuM.
  - Fossil gas: activities/exposures present for electricity generation, combined heat/cool and power (CHP), and heat generation in loans and advances, guarantees, and AuM.
